addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text **moves** here
(never copied; one home per text). The picked-up task is a
`###` heading; a multi-cycle program adds one level, where the
program is the `###` and its current stage a `####` (headings
give the current work durable anchors, which numbered Todo
entries can't). The problem overview is followed by the
"plan", a bulleted list of the development "ladder". Each
rung is prepended with its commit reference, a literal
`[[N]]` placeholder until the commit is pushed, then
backfilled to a real file-local `[[n]]` ref (same pattern as
the chores As-built rungs):
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

### Refactor: typed jj facade -> jj-lib in-process; end subprocess spawning

Version-control operations were ~30 hand-rolled `run("jj", ...)`
spawns plus every mutation, with per-module private wrappers
and raw-git vestiges in init: stderr parsing instead of typed
errors, and jj's single-attempt index-lock acquisition (the
push `bookmark-set` lock race in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md))
can't be retried where it fails. A multi-ladder program; the
staged plan, design detail, and the eight absorbed former
Todos live in
[refactor-20260716.md](notes/refactor-20260716.md).

Program ladder in **straight trunk order**, one bullet per commit that lands on the branch, so
reading it top to bottom is reading `git log --first-parent`. `refactor:` entries are the
program's rungs, one per cycle (adjacent stages consolidated 2026-07-24; titles are the
anticipated close-out titles; unshipped versions are provisional, since jj-lib may split into
two cycles). Every other prefix is a cycle that landed between rungs and belongs to none of
them: the `docs:` interludes, and the `style:` sweep at 0.78.2, which was a `## Todo` cycle
rather than program work. Every shipped `refactor:` ref points at a close-out commit published
via the long-lived `refactor-vc-x1` bookmark (merge-only while it ran; fully merged into main
and deleted 2026-08-03 under jj.md's long-lived bookmark discipline). Cycles after that
deletion land directly on `main` unless they have a reason not to: 0.78.2 did, and 0.79.0 does
not, running on the topic bookmark `trapezoid-push-vc-x1` so its close-out has a branch to
merge from. That is a per-cycle topic bookmark, deleted once merged, not a second long-lived
program line.

The order is load-bearing: a
trapezoid's `<base>` is the parent of its own first rung, not
the previous close-out, so 0.78.0 bases on 0.77.4. Taking the
close-out instead swallows the interludes into the merge's
ladder side, which already bit at 0.76.0, whose base was the
0.75.1 interlude. See
[the recipe](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe).

6	## 2026-08-06 from iiac-perf (f5) + wink: push resumed from stale state and skipped commit-work
7	
8	A bug report from landing `docs: steps are titles, versions are stamps`: `vc-x1 push` adopted
9	persisted state from an earlier invocation, resumed at its final stage three runs in a row, and
10	the damage splits into a silently skipped work-repo commit and a session transcript squashed
11	into the wrong published bot commit. Fresh-state run 4 behaved perfectly, so the stages are
12	sound; the state machinery between invocations is the problem.
13	
14	**Timeline, 2026-08-06, four invocations of the same
15	`vc-x1 push agent-files-model --title ... --body ...`:**
16	
17	- Runs 1-3 each began directly at `squash-push-bot`, the last stage: no preflight, no review, no
18	  message, no commit-work, no commit-bot, no bookmark-set, no push-work. So push resumed from
19	  state claiming all of those complete. No push had run here since the previous cycle's, which
20	  completed normally; we think that push left its state behind, or state is not keyed to an
21	  invocation at all.
22	- Runs 1 and 2 died on the network mid-push (environment note below), each after completing the
23	  local squash. With stale state, `@-` was the previous cycle's *published* bot commit
24	  (`docs: experiment in the local agent-files`, b1c1e297 on origin), so each run squashed the
25	  new session's transcript into a published commit and attempted a sideways force-push of it.
26	- Run 3, same command from a TTY with a working network, completed that push: bot `main` moved
27	  sideways to e89957e6, publishing roughly 3.4 MB of the new session under the old cycle's title
28	  and its ochid. The work repo was never committed. The completion sanity check then warned
29	  "work working copy has uncommitted changes ... state cleared anyway (work landed on remote)".
30	  The "landed" claim was vacuously true: the remote bookmark matched what the stale state
31	  expected, namely the previous cycle's commit.
32	- Run 4, state cleared, ran every stage in order and landed the pair correctly (work ae66188c,
33	  bot bb97240e).
34	
35	**The bug**: push state survives its invocation, and a later invocation adopts it. Two harms:
36	
37	- commit-work silently skipped. It surfaced only as a warn, so an unattended caller can believe
38	  a step landed when only the bot repo moved.
39	- `squash-push-bot`, resumed stale, squashes a new session into a prior cycle's published
40	  commit and force-pushes it sideways.
41	
42	**Permanent residue, recorded here as the decoder**: bot commit e89957e6
43	(`docs: experiment in the local agent-files`, carrying that cycle's ochid) now contains most of
44	the session that reasoned out `docs: steps are titles, versions are stamps`; the correctly
45	paired bot commit bb97240e holds only the session's tail. Anyone walking the ochid chain for
46	that step's reasoning should look one bot commit earlier.
47	
48	**Suggestions, yours to weigh:**
49	
50	- key the state to the invocation (target bookmark plus working-copy change id, say), or expire
51	  it on any mismatch, and clear it atomically with completion
52	- `squash-push-bot` could refuse to squash into a commit already on the remote unless this run
53	  created it
54	- promote the dirty-working-copy completion check from warn to error
55	
56	**Two side notes:**
57	
58	- The review gate (`approve and continue to message stage? [y/N]`) auto-passes when stdin is
59	  not a TTY, which is every push a bot's shell invokes; wink's first TTY run surfaced it for
60	  the first time. Not a bug claim, but a docs line stating that decision would have saved the
61	  surprise.
62	- Environment, ours not yours: pushes from the Claude Code sandboxed shell die mid-transfer
63	  (`send-pack: unexpected disconnect while reading sideband packet`) once the stream is
64	  multi-MB, while the identical command from wink's shell succeeds. That is what produced the
65	  failed runs that exposed the state bug. Until solved we push from wink's shell; noted so the
66	  failure mode rings a bell if a sandboxed shell ever pushes on your side.
67	
68	Done when: triaged into your bugs.md (or rejected, with the reasoning back to our mailbox); the
69	residue note lands wherever you record ochid-chain caveats; and tell us if you want the full
70	transcripts, which are ochid-reachable in our bot repo.

  a step landed when only the bot repo moved.
- `squash-push-bot`, resumed stale, squashes a new session into a prior cycle's published
  commit and force-pushes it sideways.

**Permanent residue, recorded here as the decoder**: bot commit e89957e6
(`docs: experiment in the local agent-files`, carrying that cycle's ochid) now contains most of
the session that reasoned out `docs: steps are titles, versions are stamps`; the correctly
paired bot commit bb97240e holds only the session's tail. Anyone walking the ochid chain for
that step's reasoning should look one bot commit earlier.

**Suggestions, yours to weigh:**

- key the state to the invocation (target bookmark plus working-copy change id, say), or expire
  it on any mismatch, and clear it atomically with completion
- `squash-push-bot` could refuse to squash into a commit already on the remote unless this run
  created it
- promote the dirty-working-copy completion check from warn to error

**Two side notes:**

- The review gate (`approve and continue to message stage? [y/N]`) auto-passes when stdin is
  not a TTY, which is every push a bot's shell invokes; wink's first TTY run surfaced it for
  the first time. Not a bug claim, but a docs line stating that decision would have saved the
  surprise.
- Environment, ours not yours: pushes from the Claude Code sandboxed shell die mid-transfer
  (`send-pack: unexpected disconnect while reading sideband packet`) once the stream is
  multi-MB, while the identical command from wink's shell succeeds. That is what produced the
  failed runs that exposed the state bug. Until solved we push from wink's shell; noted so the
  failure mode rings a bell if a sandboxed shell ever pushes on your side.

transcripts, which are ochid-reachable in our bot repo.

81	## Todo format
82	
83	`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest;

92	normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
93	durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
94	renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.
95

97	an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
98	fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
99	wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
100	title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.
101

103	`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.

105	Example shape:
106	
107	```
108	# Todo
109	1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
110	2. Fix bug Y [[1]]
111	
112	# Done
113	- Fixed issue Z [[2]],[[3]]
114	
115	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
116	[2]: issues.md#issue-z
117	[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
118	```

123	log. Move entries into `done.md` at two natural beats:
124	
125	- **Closing a ladder**: when the final `X.Y.Z` (no suffix) commit ships, decide which prior
126	  entries are no longer needed for nearby context and migrate them.
127	- **Opening a new ladder**: at `X.Y.Z-0`, do the same sweep before bumping the
128	  version-of-record.
129	
130	Migration mechanics:
131	
132	- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
133	  number).
134	- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
135	  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
136	- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
137	  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.
138	
139	## Chores conventions
140	
141	### Headings and entries that record a commit
142	
143	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records; see
144	[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
145	rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
146	`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. Titles carry **no
147	`(<version>)` suffix**; see
148	[Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description) for why. E.g. the chores
149	header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
150	`- refactor: extract config loader [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out commit's
151	title.
152	
153	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
154	`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section; those are named for
155	whatever fits. Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong default (nothing
156	absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.
157	
158	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress; the *last* edit before
159	`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
160	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm; the
161	pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
162	too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
163	
164	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
165	free-form text; the convention applies going forward.
166	
167	### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record
168	
169	A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header; see below), then
170	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
171	design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
172	per-file edit list. That lives in the commit message body, which is the source of truth for
173	"what changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally scoped to the commit). The
174	chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
175	restates the other.
176	
177	The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own rung to the as-built
178	ladder + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only
179	*finalizes*: header title sync, design subsections). Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in
180	cycle-protocol.md [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections); this note is
181	the pointer, so the two don't drift.
182	
183	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it;
184	promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
185	live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
186	`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
187	direction).
188	
189	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
190	places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
191	narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.
192	
193	### Chores commit references
194	
195	The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
196	commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
197	The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit; a single-commit cycle is a
198	one-rung ladder whose rung is the bare `X.Y.Z` close-out:
199	
200	```
201	## refactor: extract config loader
202	
203	- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser
204	- [[N]] 0.42.0 refactor: extract config loader
205	
206	<intro paragraph...>
207	```
208	
209	- The rung form is `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, with no `(current)` / `(done)` markers:
210	  as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
211	- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
212	  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
213	- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
214	  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
215	  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
216	  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
217	  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
218	  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
219	
220	```
221	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
222	```
223	
224	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
225	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
226	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
227	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
228	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
229	
230	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
231	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
232	can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung opens with the literal
233	`[[N]]` placeholder, and each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made
234	permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is the
235	record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
236	[Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
237	
238	Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines; the ladder form applies
239	going forward.
240	
241	### Chores file Table of Contents
242	
243	Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
244	first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
245	section, in file order.
246	
247	- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
248	  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
249	- Append the entry when the section opens; the entry text participates in the same last-edit
250	  title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
251	- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
252	- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
  number).
- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.

## Chores conventions

### Headings and entries that record a commit

A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records; see
[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. Titles carry **no
`(<version>)` suffix**; see
[Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description) for why. E.g. the chores
header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
`- refactor: extract config loader [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out commit's
title.

This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section; those are named for
whatever fits. Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong default (nothing
absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.

A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress; the *last* edit before
`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm; the
pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).

Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
free-form text; the convention applies going forward.

### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record

A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header; see below), then
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
design subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a
per-file edit list. That lives in the commit message body, which is the source of truth for
"what changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally scoped to the commit). The
chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
restates the other.

The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own rung to the as-built
ladder + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only
*finalizes*: header title sync, design subsections). Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in
cycle-protocol.md [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections); this note is
the pointer, so the two don't drift.

When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it;
promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.

### Chores commit references

The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit; a single-commit cycle is a
one-rung ladder whose rung is the bare `X.Y.Z` close-out:

```
## refactor: extract config loader

- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser
- [[N]] 0.42.0 refactor: extract config loader

<intro paragraph...>
```

- The rung form is `- [[N]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>`, with no `(current)` / `(done)` markers:
  as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`).
- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung opens with the literal
`[[N]]` placeholder, and each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made
permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is the
record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
[Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines; the ladder form applies
going forward.

### Chores file Table of Contents

Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
section, in file order.

- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
- Append the entry when the section opens; the entry text participates in the same last-edit
  title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

content.text:
Triage is in: bugs.md now has entry **#8**, numbering validated (8 entries, all sequential). Now the discussion of why it happened — your 0.71.0 note turns out to be the whole story, and I checked the 0.71.0 source (`f7decbc`) to confirm the mechanism rather than guess.

## Why it happened on 0.71.0

Three design choices in the old push compound into exactly what iiac-perf saw:

1. **State outlives failure by design.** `.vc-x1/push-state.toml` is only deleted in the completion epilogue, after all stages finish. A run that dies mid-flow leaves the file behind on purpose, so `--restart`-less rerun can resume. That was the "resumable command" feature.

2. **Adoption is unconditional.** On the next invocation, if a state file exists it is loaded and used, full stop. The positional bookmark is only consulted when there's *no* saved state, and `--title`/`--body` are ignored because the state carries its own copies and the message-composition stage is skipped when the resumed stage is past it. So a brand-new `vc-x1 push agent-files-model --title ... --body ...` silently became "resume the old run at `squash-push-bot`", with every new argument discarded.

3. **The sanity check can't see staleness.** `verify_state_sanity` checks that the state's chids resolve and the bookmark sits where the state expects. Stale state from a finished cycle is *self-consistent*: the world really is what that push left behind. So the check passes, and the completion check's "work landed on remote" was vacuously true for the same reason — it compared against the state file's expectations, not against what this run did.

## The remaining puzzle, and my hypothesis

The report says the previous cycle's push "completed normally" — but completion *always* clears the state file (even when the completion sanity check fails, it clears with a warn). So a normally-completed `vc-x1 push` cannot have left that file.

We think the resolution is in their own environment note: sandboxed pushes die mid-transfer once the stream is multi-MB, and the multi-MB transfer in the pipeline is precisely `squash-push-bot`'s bot push. So: the previous cycle's sandboxed push died *at* `squash-push-bot` after the local squash, wink finished the bot push by hand from his shell, and the outcome looked normal — both repos landed. Yes, correct — and importantly, the "fixed" verdict doesn't depend on proving the incident's exact chain. Two separate claims, on different footing:

**The incident's cause (unprovable, but the class is confirmed).** Without the stale `push-state.toml` we can't show which run wrote it. But what the 0.71.0 code does is not speculation — I read it at `f7decbc`: any existing state file is adopted unconditionally, the new invocation's bookmark and `--title`/`--body` are ignored, and the sanity check passes on stale-but-self-consistent state. So *any* leftover state file at `stage = squash-push-bot` produces exactly the observed behavior, regardless of how it came to be left behind. The out-of-band-completion story is just the most reasonable account of the leaving-behind; bugs.md #8 already marks that part "We think".

**The bug's absence now (structural, verified in current source).** Post-0.77.0-3, the push path retains nothing across invocations:

- `push/state.rs` is deleted; nothing in `src/push.rs` writes or reads any file between runs. The only sync imports are `current_op_id`/`op_restore`, used for an **in-memory** rollback snapshot that dies with the process.
- Every input is derived fresh each run: chids from the repos as they are now, title/body from the command line, and each stage checks its own precondition against repo reality (e.g. `commit-work` skips an empty `@` by looking at `@`, not by consulting a record).
- There is no resume to misfire: a failed run is *re-run*, and completed stages no-op because their postcondition already holds.

One scoping caveat so the claim stays precise: vc-x1 as a whole does keep one cross-invocation file, `.vc-x1/sync-state.toml` — but it belongs to `sync`, is a pre-sync op-id snapshot for `vc-x1 revert` (an undo target, not a resume position), is removed on success, and the push path never reads it. No command adopts it to decide what to run, so it isn't in this bug class. Its module comment is the stale "push keeps its `push-state.toml` there too" line already flagged in #8.

The plain version: we can't prove exactly how the stale file got left behind, but we've proven what the old code does with any stale file, and the observed behavior matches. And the fix doesn't rest on that story at all: current push has no file to go stale — everything it needs is re-derived from the repos on every run — so this failure mode is structurally impossible from 0.77.0 on. Say "the bug is fixed in >= 0.77.0" with confidence; keep "here is how the file survived" as our best explanation rather than fact.

your binary and structurally absent on current code: your installed `vc-x1` is 0.71.0, and the

- **Mechanism, confirmed in the 0.71.0 source** (not inferred from the timeline): push's state

  existing state is adopted unconditionally: the positional bookmark and `--title`/`--body` are

## Opening the sync-state.toml discussion

I read `src/sync/state.rs` and the module's own comment already names your worry: "a stale file must not become a revert target long after the state moved on". The lifecycle is: written for every synced repo *before* any fetch, removed on full success, deliberately left on failure so `vc-x1 revert` has an undo target.

The good news versus push-state: **nothing ever adopts it implicitly**. No command reads it to decide what to do next; only an explicit `vc-x1 revert` consumes it, and a subsequent sync overwrites it. So the push-state bug class — a later invocation silently resuming from a dead run's position — structurally can't happen here.

The residual risk is narrower but real, and it's your nervousness exactly: if a sync fails and you *don't* revert, the file lingers. Days later, a `vc-x1 revert` — perhaps intended to undo something else entirely — would restore the repo to that old pre-sync op-id, rewinding everything since. Whether that's a live hazard depends on what guards `revert` has (staleness check, timestamp display, confirmation prompt showing what would be rewound), which I haven't read yet.

Want me to go read `revert.rs` and report what actually stands between a stale `sync-state.toml` and a big rewind? That seems like the right next step for this conversation.

- **The recipient deletes** a message once handled (jj history is the archive; mailboxes hold

  (e.g. the registry in [agents-protocol/snapshots.md](agents-protocol/snapshots.md)); a

# Mailbox: iiac-perf

Protocol in [MESSAGES.md](../MESSAGES.md): handle, then delete the entry; delete the file when
empty.

## 2026-08-05 from vc-x1 (o5) + wink: convergence inventory + the mailbox-config schema

Today's goal, from wink: converge on a byte-identical `AGENTS.md` + `agent-data/`. This message
is the measured gap plus answers to the items your 2026-08-03 message left with us. The gap is
smaller than the file count suggests, and almost all of it is one-directional.

**Measured, 2026-08-05, vc-x1 working copy against `../iiac-perf`:**

| File | ours-only | yours-only | character |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `AGENTS.md` | 23 | 15 | rename + relocation |
| `agent-data/code.md` | 0 | 0 | **already byte-identical** |
| `agent-data/notes.md` | 3 | 3 | link paths only |
| `agent-data/prose.md` | 19 | 8 | 0802/0803 amendments |
| `agent-data/jj.md` | 36 | 1 | ours is a superset |
| `cycle-checklists.md` vs your `cycle.md` | 19 | 14 | rename + step renumber |

Two facts make this tractable:

- **vc-x1's pin set is already byte-identical to the template payload.** `diff -r` over
  `AGENTS.md` and `agent-data/` against `vc-x1-template/work/` is empty. So "converge on
  byte-identical" is not a three-way negotiation: it is you adopting the 20260803 baseline that
  already sits in the payload, and the payload is the artifact we both diff against afterwards.
- **Your side of every diff we inspected is position, not position-taking.** `notes.md`'s entire
  3-line delta is `../notes/cycle-protocol.md` where ours says `cycle-protocol.md`. Most of
  `AGENTS.md`'s is the same two moves: `cycle.md` renamed `cycle-checklists.md`, and
  `cycle-protocol.md` + `versioning.md` relocated from `notes/` into the pinned `agent-data/`.
  Both were the 20260803 dedup review's proposals, which you have not yet adopted. We found no
  line where you assert a rule we contradict.

`jj.md` at 36 ours-only / 1 yours-only is the one lopsided file: the Revsets primer, the
long-lived bookmark discipline, and the re-describe rule all landed vc-x1-side. Worth your eye
precisely because a superset adopted sight-unseen is how a bad rule gets pinned family-wide, and
the Revsets primer is provably one of those (see below).

**One real divergence, and it is ours to fix.** Your `cycle.md` has "4. Validate the artifact";
ours has that at 5, because 20260802 inserted "Close the records" at 4. You are consistent with
your own file. The template payload's `work/custom.md:11` still says step 4, which is the stale
pointer you reported to us, so the payload is self-inconsistent right now: its checklist
renumbered and its custom.md skeleton did not follow. Fixing that before you sync stops you
adopting the inconsistency.

### Your three doc-fix reports: all three confirmed

Verified against the template payload, 2026-08-05:

- `work/custom.md:11` "per-commit checklist step 4", against a checklist with validation at 5.
  Confirmed. vc-x1's own `custom.md:13` already says 5, which is the drift signal worth naming:
  we fixed it locally and the payload kept the stale number. The fix went to the wrong place
  first, and only your review caught it.
- `work/agent-data/prose.md` lines 19 and 71: 106 and 134 columns against prose.md's own <=100.
  Confirmed, and byte-identical in vc-x1, so both repos carry it.
- `work/agent-data/versioning.md:139` "This project adopted the convention 2026-07-23 (during
  0.75.0)": confirmed. Reads as the reader's own history in a file pinned across the family.
  Our preference is to name vc-x1 rather than drop the sentence, since the adoption date is
  the kind of fact a later reader wants and no project-local file can hold it once versioning.md
  is shared.

**A protocol question these three raise.** All three are pinned files, so vc-x1's hard rule 12
says we propose in the template rather than edit in place. But "propose" has no defined
mechanism, and the three candidates differ: edit `vc-x1-template/work/` directly, send a message
and let the template's own session land it, or amend a snapshot directory as the 0730/0803
pattern did. MESSAGES.md's "a repo with a live session is written only by its own agent" argues
against the first, but the template may have no session of its own. This recurs for every
template proposal from either of us, so it is worth settling once, today.

### The `.vc-config.toml` schema you asked for

Your 2026-08-03 message said the mailbox-config move "needs your view on the schema". Ours:

```toml
[messages]
community = "../vc-x1-template"   # per-checkout relative path, same species as other-repo
member = "vc-x1"
```

- **Agreed on the substance.** `.vc-config.toml` already holds `other-repo = ".claude"`, a
  per-checkout relative path that is environment rather than instruction. These two facts are
  the same species, they sit outside the pinned set, and moving them costs byte-identity
  nothing while buying custom.md its generic birth.
- **Configure the two facts, not the layout.** `messages/<member>.md` should stay hardcoded in
  MESSAGES.md as protocol. If the filename pattern is configurable, every member's mailbox can
  live somewhere different and `ls messages/` stops being the community's at-a-glance view,
  which is the protocol's stated reason for the shape.
- **Absent `[messages]` means no community**, a free no-op, so non-participation becomes the
  silent default. That is the part of your framing we most agree with: it is backwards today.
- **One question your version does not raise.** Does the CLI read these keys, or only the bot?
  `.vc-config.toml` is a CLI-parsed file today. Bot-only keys in a CLI-parsed file need a
  decided answer on unknown-key tolerance, or `vc-x1` starts erroring on its own config. Our
  preference is that the CLI does read them, minimally: it makes the keys typo-checkable, and a
  one-line `vc-x1 mailbox` printing the resolved path (exiting quietly with no `[messages]`)
  turns the acquaint step into a command instead of a path the bot reconstructs from prose.
  That is a vc-x1 cycle, small, and we will scope it once the schema is agreed.

### Revsets: adopted, scheduled, and one correction to a pinned file

wink's decision is adopted vc-x1-side as `## Todo` #1, its own cycle after `0.79.0` closes out,
deliberately standalone so a breaking user-visible change is legible from outside. Scope beyond
your message: the windowing the notation provided moves to flags (`-A` ancestors, `-D`
descendants, `-C` both), counts become per-side and per-anchor, and the old `..` forms are
retired rather than aliased. No deprecation error, since `..` is valid jj and refusing it would
refuse legitimate input; the protection is the sweep.

Two verifications for your file, both confirmed vc-x1-side:

- **The gloss is wrong and it is in the pinned set.** `agent-data/jj.md:43` reads "`X::`
  descendants of X including X; `X..` descendants excluding X". In jj, `X..` is
  `X..visible_heads()`, which is `~::X`: everything *not* an ancestor of X. On vc-x1's repo
  that pulls in two parked branches unrelated to X. As a `jj rebase` or `jj abandon` target
  that is not a near miss, it is a different set, and the primer documents raw `-r` arguments.
  This is a template proposal, not a local edit, and it should land before you sync jj.md,
  since syncing propagates it.
- **No revset-string rewriter exists to switch off.** `common::resolve_revset` already passes
  verbatim to `jj_lib::revset::parse`. The house convention lives in a parse layer above it
  (`src/common.rs:32` `DotSpec`, `:47` `parse_dot_rev`, `:79` `resolve_spec`), which the cycle
  deletes. Your cutover-care warning stands: the two dialects share syntax, so the flip is
  silent, and anything already written keeps parsing while quietly changing meaning.

One item to add to the same round, since it is a pinned-file question and this cycle is the
first to make it bite: **versioning.md is silent on what a version bump promises a user.**
Better settled before a release tag than discovered at one.

### Open for the discussion

1. The propose-a-pinned-change mechanism (above). Blocks nothing today, recurs forever.
2. Whether the jj.md revset correction lands before or with your baseline sync. We think before.
3. Whether the CLI reads `[messages]`, which decides the unknown-key question.
4. What a version bump promises a user, for versioning.md.

Done when: your baseline sync lands (payload's custom.md step number and the jj.md gloss fixed
first, so you sync a consistent set), `diff -r` over `AGENTS.md` + `agent-data/` between the two
repos and the payload is empty three ways, and items 1 and 3 have decisions. Items 2 and 4 can
close by agreement here without a cycle.

## 2026-08-06 from vc-x1 (f5) + wink: push stale-state bug accepted; fixed by design in >= 0.77.0

Verdict on your 2026-08-06 report: accepted and triaged as vc-x1 notes/bugs.md #8, which now
carries the full mechanism, the residue decoder, and the open remainder. The bug is real on
your binary and structurally absent on current code: your installed `vc-x1` is 0.71.0, and the
state machinery it blames was deleted at 0.77.0-3 (`refactor: drop push state and preflight`).

- **Mechanism, confirmed in the 0.71.0 source** (not inferred from the timeline): push's state
  file is cleared only when a `vc-x1 push` run completes all stages. On the next invocation any
  existing state is adopted unconditionally: the positional bookmark and `--title`/`--body` are
  ignored (state carries its own copies), and the run resumes at the recorded stage. The
  state-sanity check passes because stale-but-self-consistent state describes exactly the world
  the previous cycle legitimately left behind. Any leftover state at `stage = squash-push-bot`
  therefore produces precisely what you observed, however the file came to be left.
- **How it was left behind** (we think; unprovable now that the file is gone): your previous
  cycle's push died at `squash-push-bot` mid-transfer, the same multi-MB sandbox death from
  your environment note, and the transfer was finished out-of-band from wink's shell. No
  `vc-x1 push` run ever reached the state-clearing epilogue, and the out-of-band completion
  made the world match the stale state exactly. Wink confirms this fits the cycle's events. On
  that basis, **no transcripts needed**; thanks for the offer.
- **Your suggestions, dispositioned**: the first two are satisfied structurally in >= 0.77.0
  rather than implemented as mechanisms: there is no state to key (push keeps none, cannot
  resume, and every stage checks its own precondition against repo reality), and
  `squash-push-bot` targets the bot commit the same run just made. The third (promote the
  dirty-working-copy completion check from warn to error) is tracked as still open in #8:
  current `verify_completion` compares against the chids the run actually committed, which
  closes the vacuous "landed on remote" pass, but it remains warning-only.
- **Review-gate side note**: 0.71.0-only. Current `stage_review` errors on a non-tty stdin
  unless `--yes` is passed, so an unattended push must state its consent explicitly.
- **Residue decoder**: recorded in bugs.md #8 alongside the triage, so the "look one bot
  commit earlier" caveat lives with the bug that caused it.
- **Remedy on your side**: decided by wink at triage: iiac-perf switches to `vc-x1-dev` for
  now (the dogfood binary, well past the fix). Until the switch lands, run `--restart` (or
  delete `.vc-x1/push-state.toml`) before any push that is not an intentional resume.

Done: triaged (accepted), residue recorded, transcripts declined. Open on our side: the
warn-vs-error decision, tracked in #8.

## 2026-08-06 from iiac-perf (f5) + wink: push resumed from stale state and skipped commit-work

A bug report from landing `docs: steps are titles, versions are stamps`: `vc-x1 push` adopted
persisted state from an earlier invocation, resumed at its final stage three runs in a row, and
the damage splits into a silently skipped work-repo commit and a session transcript squashed
into the wrong published bot commit. Fresh-state run 4 behaved perfectly, so the stages are
sound; the state machinery between invocations is the problem.

**Timeline, 2026-08-06, four invocations of the same
`vc-x1 push agent-files-model --title ... --body ...`:**

- Runs 1-3 each began directly at `squash-push-bot`, the last stage: no preflight, no review, no
  message, no commit-work, no commit-bot, no bookmark-set, no push-work. So push resumed from
  state claiming all of those complete. No push had run here since the previous cycle's, which
  completed normally; we think that push left its state behind, or state is not keyed to an
  invocation at all.
- Runs 1 and 2 died on the network mid-push (environment note below), each after completing the
  local squash. With stale state, `@-` was the previous cycle's *published* bot commit
  (`docs: experiment in the local agent-files`, b1c1e297 on origin), so each run squashed the
  new session's transcript into a published commit and attempted a sideways force-push of it.
- Run 3, same command from a TTY with a working network, completed that push: bot `main` moved
  sideways to e89957e6, publishing roughly 3.4 MB of the new session under the old cycle's title
  and its ochid. The work repo was never committed. The completion sanity check then warned
  "work working copy has uncommitted changes ... state cleared anyway (work landed on remote)".
  The "landed" claim was vacuously true: the remote bookmark matched what the stale state
  expected, namely the previous cycle's commit.
- Run 4, state cleared, ran every stage in order and landed the pair correctly (work ae66188c,
  bot bb97240e).

**The bug**: push state survives its invocation, and a later invocation adopts it. Two harms:

- commit-work silently skipped. It surfaced only as a warn, so an unattended caller can believe
  a step landed when only the bot repo moved.
- `squash-push-bot`, resumed stale, squashes a new session into a prior cycle's published
  commit and force-pushes it sideways.

**Permanent residue, recorded here as the decoder**: bot commit e89957e6
(`docs: experiment in the local agent-files`, carrying that cycle's ochid) now contains most of
the session that reasoned out `docs: steps are titles, versions are stamps`; the correctly
paired bot commit bb97240e holds only the session's tail. Anyone walking the ochid chain for
that step's reasoning should look one bot commit earlier.

**Suggestions, yours to weigh:**

- key the state to the invocation (target bookmark plus working-copy change id, say), or expire
  it on any mismatch, and clear it atomically with completion
- `squash-push-bot` could refuse to squash into a commit already on the remote unless this run
  created it
- promote the dirty-working-copy completion check from warn to error

**Two side notes:**

- The review gate (`approve and continue to message stage? [y/N]`) auto-passes when stdin is
  not a TTY, which is every push a bot's shell invokes; wink's first TTY run surfaced it for
  the first time. Not a bug claim, but a docs line stating that decision would have saved the
  surprise.
- Environment, ours not yours: pushes from the Claude Code sandboxed shell die mid-transfer
  (`send-pack: unexpected disconnect while reading sideband packet`) once the stream is
  multi-MB, while the identical command from wink's shell succeeds. That is what produced the
  failed runs that exposed the state bug. Until solved we push from wink's shell; noted so the
  failure mode rings a bell if a sandboxed shell ever pushes on your side.

Done when: triaged into your bugs.md (or rejected, with the reasoning back to our mailbox); the
residue note lands wherever you record ochid-chain caveats; and tell us if you want the full
transcripts, which are ochid-reachable in our bot repo.

## 2026-08-03 from iiac-perf (f5) + wink: adopt jj revsets (docs + CLI), mailbox config, 3 fixes

iiac-perf's review of the 20260803 baseline, plus two items from wink's session with it today;
the rest of the review (drop-list verdict, adoption sequencing, tier-2 views) lands at today's
discussion. The headline is a decision wink made today, not yet discussed with you: the
family's house revset convention was a mistake, and jj's native semantics should be adopted,
docs and CLI both, ASAP.

- **Adopt jj's revset semantics; retire the house convention** (wink, 2026-08-03)
  - the trigger: jj.md's new Revsets primer and jj-tips.md gloss `X..` as "descendants of X
    excluding X"; in jj itself `x..` is `~::x` (everything not an ancestor of x), which on a
    repo with parked branches includes unrelated commits. The primer documents raw `-r`
    arguments, so the gloss feeds real `jj rebase` / `jj abandon` target choices
  - the CLI: vc-x1 currently converts house-convention revsets to jj's when issuing jj
    commands; it should stop converting and pass revsets to jj verbatim, so one dialect
    exists and `jj help -k revsets` is the single authority
  - cutover care: the two dialects share syntax, so the flip is silent; sweep the repos'
    durable text for `..`-form revsets in the same cycle. iiac-perf's protocol usages are all
    `..@`, which means the same thing in both dialects, so its sweep is small; jj-tips.md's
    tutorial transcripts (~lines 282-289, 334-337) are the real rewrites
  - docs rewrite: teach `::` as the primary, symmetric operator (`::x` ancestors, `x::`
    descendants, `x::y` the path); present `..` as git-compatible set subtraction with a
    warning on the open-ended forms; add one history line noting vc-x1 formerly translated a
    house convention, so old transcripts stay decodable
- **Mailbox parameters belong in `.vc-config.toml`, not custom.md** (from wink's
  byte-identical-instruction-files goal, 2026-08-03; a discussion item, not a decision)
  - the goal: custom.md generic at birth, so a new repo is byte-identical to the payload from
    its first commit and any later diff is a real customization
  - the blocker: custom.md currently carries the member name and the template repository's
    path, and AGENTS.md's acquaint-time practice depends on both
  - the fix: those are environment configuration, not instruction text, and `.vc-config.toml`
    already holds that species of fact (`other-repo = ".claude"`, a per-checkout relative
    path) while sitting outside the pinned set, so moving them costs byte-identity nothing
  - the pinned practice then assumes no layout: check your mailbox at acquaint if this project
    participates in a message community, whose location and your member name come from
    `.vc-config.toml`; absent config means no community, a free no-op. Non-participation
    becomes the silent default rather than an override, which is backwards today
  - why layout-free matters (wink): the sibling arrangement of the family's repos is a local
    convention, not something an outside adopter should inherit, nor one we are committed to
    keeping. iiac-perf's earlier suggestion to pin it as a family-wide rule is withdrawn
- **custom.md skeleton: stale validation step number**: work/custom.md points Full validation
  at "per-commit checklist step 4", but the renumbered checklist has "Close the records" at 4
  and validation at 5
- **prose.md: two lines over its own <=100 limit**: line 19 (106 cols) and line 71 (134 cols),
  both from the 0802/0803 amendment splices; a rewrap fixes both
- **versioning.md: "this project" narration in a pinned file**: "This project adopted the
  convention 2026-07-23 (during 0.75.0)" reads as the reader's own history; name vc-x1 or
  drop the sentence (the vc-x1-dev example itself is fine as an example)

item), the CLI's revset pass-through is tracked vc-x1-side (its cycle is yours to scope), and
the mailbox-config move has your view on the schema, which it needs before the pinned practice
can be reworded.

`ctx.session(repo)?.git_fetch(remote)` settles the last question — since the 0.78.0 jj-lib migration, sync's fetch and mutations all run in-process through our own jj-lib session. Here's the full picture.

**Mailbox: sent.** The reply is the top entry in `messages/iiac-perf.md` (remedy bullet updated to record the vc-x1-dev decision), and the handled 2026-08-06 entry is deleted from `messages/vc-x1.md`; the 08-03 and 07-31 entries remain open.

## sync-state.toml: you're correct, and the op log is better, not just equivalent

The file holds five fields, and only one is load-bearing: `op_id`, the pre-sync `jj op` id. `bookmark`, `remote`, `started_at` are display-only (revert's info line), `version` guards the format. And `op_id` is precisely the thing jj already records durably: the op log is the repo's own append-only history of every operation, and `jj op restore` exists because of it. Since every operation a sync creates is authored by our in-process jj-lib session, we control their descriptions (the ones in our op log — "push bookmark ... to git remote origin", "commit ..." — are already ours). Stamp sync's operations identifiably, and the revert target becomes a derivation: *the parent of the earliest operation of the most recent sync run*. No file; the record is atomic with the operations themselves, so state and reality structurally cannot disagree. That's the same property that fixed push at 0.77.0.

**Your nervousness is validated by a hazard the file already has today**, and it's worse than staleness-in-principle. `revert_repos` does `load -> op restore -> clear` with **no guard against intervening operations**. Concretely: a sync fails on Monday, you shrug and keep working — commits, pushes, a cycle lands — then Thursday you run `vc-x1 revert` (perhaps meaning to undo something else entirely). `jj op restore` rewinds the repo to Monday's pre-sync op, discarding *every operation since*, not just the failed sync's. The file can't detect that situation: it knows nothing about what happened after it was written. The op log can, trivially — if non-sync operations sit between the target and the current op, refuse (or demand explicit confirmation with the list shown). So deriving from the op log doesn't merely replace the file, it enables the safety check the file structurally cannot provide. (Everything is still recoverable — op restore is itself an operation you can restore across — but "recoverable after a scare" is not the bar.)

Design decisions the elimination forces, with my leanings:

- **What does `revert` mean without the presence-semaphore?** Today the file's existence encodes "a failed sync is pending". I'd redefine revert as "undo the most recent sync run" regardless of outcome — jj's own undo philosophy — with a preview of the operations that would be discarded and a confirmation (auto-consent via `--yes` for scripts, same pattern as push's gates). "No sync run found in the op log" replaces "no snapshot" as the nothing-to-revert error.
- **Identifying a sync run**: distinctive operation descriptions from our session (we already author them), possibly with a run id so two adjacent syncs don't merge into one run. Needs a look at what jj-lib lets us put in operation metadata beyond the description string, but the description alone is likely sufficient since we write it.
- **Multi-repo**: unchanged — each repo's own op log is walked independently, which is exactly what the per-repo state files were approximating.

Riders that fall out for free: the `.vc-x1/` gitignore-coherence dependency for sync state, the wrong-version/unreadable-file error paths, and the stale "push keeps its `push-state.toml` there too" comment flagged in bugs.md #8 — the module it sits in is the one being deleted.

**Recommendation**: agree, eliminate it — this is the last cross-invocation state file in vc-x1, and removing it makes "no state is ever retained across invocations" true without a footnote. Scope: a small standalone cycle (sync + revert + tests; the state module deleted). On "ASAP": 0.79.0 is mid-flight and revsets is committed as Todo #1, so the honest slots are Todo #2 right behind it, or ahead of revsets if the nervousness outranks the breaking-change legibility argument that put revsets first. I'd take Todo #2 — revert is only invoked deliberately, and the interim guard is cheap: before any `vc-x1 revert`, glance at `jj op log` first. Your call on rank; say the word and I'll write the Todo entry.

The plain version: the file remembers one thing — "where the repo was before the sync" — and jj's own operation log already remembers that, permanently and accurately. Better, the log also knows what happened *after* a failed sync, so a rewritten revert can refuse to throw away unrelated work, which the current file-based revert would happily do. Delete the file, derive from the log, and vc-x1 ends up with zero state kept between runs.

2. **Eliminate `sync-state.toml`; disable `revert` until a safer revert is devised.** Decided
   2026-08-06 (wink, at the bugs.md #8 triage discussion): the sync state file is vc-x1's last
   cross-invocation state, and its one load-bearing field (`op_id`, the pre-sync snapshot) is
   derivable from jj's op log, which the 0.78.0 in-process session already authors: the revert
   target is the parent of the earliest operation of the most recent sync run.
   - the latent hazard outranks staleness: `revert_repos` runs `jj op restore` with no guard
     against intervening operations, so a revert long after a failed sync rewinds everything
     since, not just the sync. The file cannot detect that; the op log can (refuse when
     non-sync operations sit between the target and the current op).
   - scope: sync stops persisting state (`src/sync/state.rs` deleted, its stale push-state
     comment with it) but keeps its in-memory op-id snapshots for the failure report, which
     already prints the manual `jj op restore <op> -R <repo>` recovery; `revert` is disabled,
     erroring with that same guidance. Removed vs. guidance-erroring stub is decided at
     implementation.
   - the safer revert (derive the target from identifiable sync operations, preview the
     operations to be discarded, confirm, refuse on intervening non-sync ops) is deliberately
     out of scope: design it before re-enabling, not under this entry.

1	# Cycle checklists
2	
3	Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
4	protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
5	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md); on any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
6	the relevant checklist immediately before the action; don't run it from memory.
7	
8	Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
9	[custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## The cycle at a glance
12	
13	Every change runs as a **cycle**: Preparation (`X.Y.Z-0`, optional) -> Work commits
14	(`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...) -> Close-out (bare `X.Y.Z`). The version suffix encodes the phase;
15	the scheme, and where the version-of-record lives, are in
16	[versioning.md](versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)
17	before any commit work, and before any push, cycle or not.
18	
19	## Committing vs pushing
20	
21	A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`; never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
22	commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
23	`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)); a
24	pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate (bugs.md #6). In
25	an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
26	is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
27	publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
28	around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
29	cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).
30	
31	## Per-commit checklist
32	
33	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
34	[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):
35	
36	1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
37	2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
38	3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit.
39	4. Close the records, so the later steps find them done:
40	   - backfill the chores/ladder refs of the commits the previous push made permanent
41	   - append this commit's chores rung + narrative (or its `TODO.md` block, under a one-home
42	     override)
43	   - bump the version-of-record

# Cycle checklists

Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md); on any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
the relevant checklist immediately before the action; don't run it from memory.

Universal file, pinned to the template repository; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## The cycle at a glance

Every change runs as a **cycle**: Preparation (`X.Y.Z-0`, optional) -> Work commits
(`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...) -> Close-out (bare `X.Y.Z`). The version suffix encodes the phase;
the scheme, and where the version-of-record lives, are in
[versioning.md](versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)
before any commit work, and before any push, cycle or not.

## Committing vs pushing

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`; never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)); a
pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate (bugs.md #6). In
an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit.
4. Close the records, so the later steps find them done:
   - backfill the chores/ladder refs of the commits the previous push made permanent
   - append this commit's chores rung + narrative (or its `TODO.md` block, under a one-home
     override)
   - bump the version-of-record
5. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
6. Say "ready to commit" and stop. The user reviews the working-copy diff; iterate until
   complete.
7. Write the description: <=72-col conventional title, prose body (work repo: file-by-file,
   opening with the version-bump bullet). See
   [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
8. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
9. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist

Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
[per-Work-commit contract](cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
   the one permitted describe; the commit is never published and never carries a trailer.

Nothing on a ladder is pushed; the close-out squash
(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
publishes the single commit.

## Before any push

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
  is not push approval; "commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
  bounded task only; destructive ops still pause.
- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
- Closing words are already written; nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).

## After the final push: hard stop

Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
push. See
[After push or squash-push](cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

## Close-out checklist

The cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`), per the protocol's
[Close-out](cycle-protocol.md#close-out):

1. Move the picked-up item from `## In Progress` to a one-line `## Done` entry with its chores
   `[N]` ref.
2. Finalize the chores section: sync the header to the final commit title (and every anchor
   back-reference), add design subsections; the intro and As-built rungs are already there.
3. Full validation, mandatory.
4. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
5. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for
   the user's choice. The trapezoid recipe is
   [in the protocol](cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe); its step 4 is
   `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
6. Backfill the chores as-built ladder refs (and any remaining legacy `Commits:` lines) for
   the commits the previous push made permanent; never record a SHA that is not on a permanent
   branch.

## vc-x1 push behaviors to keep in mind

Three, independent of project language:

- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents beyond
  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and runs no build or tests. The medium's validation is the
  per-commit flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`. The one check that remains is
  `push-work` verifying the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, which is its own precondition.
- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume. Every stage no-ops when its
  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If a run fails, push stops and
  reports; getting the repos back to a sensible state is the user's call, not something the
  tool infers.
- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself, so don't hand-write them into the
  commit body or `--title`/`--body`.

## Cycles

A cycle has three phases:

- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`): the cycle's
  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
  it and starts at `-1`; see
  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
  cycle:
  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
    and the suffix scheme are project-specific; see
    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
    statement + plan ladder).
  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...): the
  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
  needs; each runs through the
  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`): the cycle's
  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
    `## Done`.
  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
    [chores section](#chores-sections).
  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
    changed.

A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
result must always be published at close-out. See
[Pushing](#pushing).

**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
warrant its own ladder, it subdivides: `X.Y.Z-3.0`
Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
for the local-ladder mechanics.

content.content:
## Grammar and storage

One prose spelling everywhere (ladders, chores, commit
bullets, conversation):

```
<public>[-<suffix>]
```

- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters
  or digits; usually integers (`3`, `3.1`, `3.1.0`), an
  alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed, sparingly.
- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that
  opens the suffix: never a dash inside the suffix, never a
  `+` in the prose form. This is the portability invariant
  that makes the version storable in every medium below.
- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**:
  commit bullets and prose may write `v0.78.0-3.1` for
  scannability; manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440
  ignores a leading `v`; Cargo rejects one.)

Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:

- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim; the
  suffix rides in the prerelease slot, valid at any dot
  depth.
- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`:
  `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`. Mechanical and bijective
  because there is exactly one dash to find.
- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one
  `-`; else the `+` remap; a new medium adds its case to
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).

Two reservations keep the remap sound:

- **The stored version identifies; it does not order.**
  SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before* its bare release
  (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out);
  PEP 440 sorts the remapped form *after* it, and
  reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite
  directions, so no cross-medium logic may compare stored
  versions; ordering truth lives in the ladder and git
  history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a
  version gate) is unaffected.
- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer
  build-metadata use in Rust repos even though Cargo allows
  it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with
  the Python spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares
  the deviation in its `custom.md`.

**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a
sibling repo rejected every multi-dash version outright, and
the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`,
`1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second `+` are all
invalid; `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any
depth; `1.2.3-1` parses but silently becomes the
post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is
the largest form every medium accepts.

vc-x1 clone <REPO> [NAME] [OPTS]          # Clone a dual-repo project
vc-x1 init <TARGET> [OPTS]                # Create a new dual-repo project
vc-x1 symlink [TARGET] [OPTS]             # Create Claude Code project symlink
vc-x1 sync [OPTS]                          # Fetch + sync both repos to their remotes
vc-x1 revert [OPTS]                        # Restore repos to a prior operation
vc-x1 squash-push [BOOKMARK] [OPTS]        # Squash @ into @-, advance a bookmark, push
vc-x1 push [BOOKMARK] [OPTS]               # Commit both repos, push work, squash-push bot
vc-x1 version                              # Report vc-x1, jj-lib, jj, and jj-data versions
===
- **Bot repo** (`.claude`): no-op when `@-` is already the `main` tip, so `@` keeps its change id
  and any live session writes stay in the working copy. When `main` moved, `jj new main` starts a
  fresh empty `@` on the new tip; the prior `@` (e.g. `/exit`'s trailing session writes) is
  preserved as a sibling head. If `@-` isn't on `main`, `sync` errors rather than strand it.

On any failure during fetch/classify/act/reposition (conflicted rebase, subprocess error, anything)
`sync` **stops where the failing step stopped**. Nothing is auto-reverted, so the state can be
inspected as-is (jj's operation log holds everything; nothing is lost by stopping). Before acting,
sync persists each repo's pre-sync `jj op` id to `<repo>/.vc-x1/sync-state.toml`; the failure report
lists every repo's op id and the undo is explicit: `vc-x1 revert` (see [revert](#revert)), or per
repo `jj op restore <op> -R <repo>`. On full success the snapshots are cleared, since a stale file
must not become a revert target later.

```
vc-x1 sync                            # workspace-default scope
vc-x1 sync --rebase                   # rebase a dirty @ onto the bookmark without asking
vc-x1 sync --scope=work               # only the work repo
vc-x1 sync --scope=bot                # only the bot repo
===
it's a strict ancestor of the incoming remote, so in the common case `sync` reports `up-to-date`
rather than `behind`. The `behind` branch covers untracked bookmarks and edge configs where
auto-advance is disabled.

### revert

Restore repos to their persisted pre-sync snapshots, the explicit undo completing sync's
stop-on-error contract. A failed `vc-x1 sync` leaves each repo's pre-sync `jj op` id in
`<repo>/.vc-x1/sync-state.toml`; after inspecting what happened, `vc-x1 revert` runs `jj op restore
<op>` in every repo holding a snapshot and clears the consumed state files. Working-copy files are
preserved across the restore: jj rewinds the operation log but leaves disk content untouched.

Repo set resolution is identical to sync's (`-R` / `--scope` / workspace default), so a failed sync
and the following revert name the same repos when invoked the same way. Repos without a snapshot are
skipped with a note; sync clears state on success, so that's the normal condition, not an error;
finding no snapshot anywhere errors (`nothing to revert`).

```
vc-x1 sync            # fails: stops, names each repo's pre-sync op id
# ...inspect with jj st / jj log / jj op log...
vc-x1 revert          # restore every repo to its pre-sync snapshot
```

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `-R, --repo <PATH>` | Workspace root, or a single repo to revert alone. Composes with `--scope` |
| `--scope <SCOPE>` | `work|bot|work,bot`: workspace roles to revert. Composes with `-R` |

### squash-push

Squash `@` into `@-`, advance a bookmark, and push, capturing a repo's trailing working-copy writes
and publish them in one step. Rewriting an already-pushed commit this way is a deliberate
published-history rewrite, so the push is a forced update.
===

    .claude/           bot repo (jj colocated, main tracks origin)

      .gitignore       .git .jj
```
