content.text:
The instinct is right — today's session even produced the evidence for it (the `cargo install` on this line silently replaced the 0.79.0-0 binary with 0.78.3). But the proposal splits into two halves with very different costs, because of one structural fact: **"on main" is not a property of a commit's content**. The name lives in Cargo.toml, which is committed content; whether that commit sits on main is a property of refs, and it changes after the fact — every cycle's commits are off-main today and on main after landing, byte-identical. So a name *in the manifest* can't track branch location without a rename commit at every landing, guaranteed Cargo.toml/Cargo.lock merge conflicts between every pair of lines, and a manifest that is wrong on one side of every merge. That's why versioning.md's current convention makes the name **constant** and moves the main-ness distinction into the *act of installing* — which, notably, already encodes your rule: the promotion path is "a separate clone built at the chosen commit" — in practice a main commit — "with the plain name". "On main = `vc-x1`" is the existing promotion semantics; what's genuinely new in your proposal is the `X`.

So the workable form keeps the manifest name constant (`vc-x1-dev`) and applies your convention at install time:

- **`vc-x1`**: only ever built from a landed main SHA, by the explicit promotion act. The clone path also fixes the banner blemish we just hit — a promoted binary that self-identifies as `vc-x1 0.78.3` instead of `vc-x1-dev 0.78.3`, because the name is baked at compile time from the manifest the clone edits.
- **`vc-x1-dev`**: the default dogfood install, as today — the single-line case, which is most days.
- **`vc-x1-devX`**: when multiple lines are genuinely in flight, differentiate at install — copy to a suffixed name, `X` = the topic bookmark's short name (`vc-x1-dev-dropsync`, `vc-x1-dev-trapezoid`). The per-commit flow's install stays untouched; the copy is the same one-line act as promotion. `-V` still reports the exact rung either way, so `X` is for coexistence, not identification.

What the install-time version costs versus yours: it's a habit, not an enforcement — nothing stops a stale `vc-x1-devX` from lingering or a line from forgetting to differentiate. I'd accept that; the alternative (manifest-encoded names) buys enforcement at the price of merge conflicts forever, and if the habit ever proves too weak, a `vc-x1 install` subcommand that knows the current bookmark could mechanize it later.

Two process notes: versioning.md is pinned, so this is a **template proposal**, not a local edit (hard rule 12) — it belongs in the baseline discussion with iiac-perf, and today gave it a clean evidence trail (the clobbered 0.79.0-0 install, and the promoted binary's wrong banner). And it slots into the still-open "what does a version bump promise a user" mailbox item, since both are about what the family may rely on from an installed binary.

The plain version: your rule is the right *meaning*, but branch location can't live in a file that gets merged between branches — so express the rule in how binaries get installed and named on disk, not in the package name: plain `vc-x1` only from landed main by deliberate act, `vc-x1-dev` for the everyday single line, a bookmark-suffixed copy when lines multiply.

content.text:
I see it — you want the name to be *born* correct so installation is naturally correct. Two mechanical facts break the literal version of it, and it's worth being concrete because one of them is a safety inversion, not a style objection.

**The boundary commit can't satisfy the invariant.** Landing on main here isn't a rebase that could edit the manifest in flight — the push fast-forwards `main` (or merges) to the *same commit* that sat on the branch. Whatever `name =` that commit carries, it carries in both worlds: authored on a branch (should say `vc-x1-devX`), permanent on main moments later (should say `vc-x1`), byte-identical. The only way "on main => vc-x1" holds is if every close-out commit flips the name as part of close-out and every cycle-open flips it back — two manifest renames per cycle as ritual. (I'll concede a point from my last message: the *merge-conflict* cost of that churn is nearly free, since the version bump already touches the same files every commit. The churn isn't the real problem.)

**The real problem: the mandatory install gate would clobber stable with unpublished code.** Full validation's step 4 is `cargo install --path . --locked`, run *before* the push, on every close-out. Under the rename-at-close-out scheme, that's the moment the manifest says `vc-x1` — so the validation gate itself overwrites the consumers' binary with a commit that hasn't been reviewed for push, may still be amended, and might never land. That's precisely the hazard the dev-name convention was built to prevent ("a mid-cycle install never clobbers the binary consumers are running"), reintroduced systematically at the most sensitive moment of every cycle. The escape hatches all collapse back to where we started: skip install at close-out (then the close-out is the one unvalidated commit), or install to a staging root and copy after the push lands (an explicit post-landing act — the current convention with extra steps).

Smaller but real: every documented command that names the package or binary breaks or forks — `cargo update -p vc-x1-dev` in custom.md, "invoke `vc-x1-dev`, never `vc-x1`" in the instructions, and with `-devX` per line, the bots can no longer be told one binary name at all; each session would first have to resolve `X`.

There is one cargo-native mechanism that gets close to "installing gives you the proper name": declare **two `[[bin]]` targets** over the same `main.rs`, `vc-x1` and `vc-x1-dev`, constant in the manifest. The flow installs with `--bin vc-x1-dev`; promotion is `cargo install --path . --locked --bin vc-x1` at the landed main SHA — correct name, correct banner, no rename, no clone. Its sharp edge: a bare `cargo install --path .` now installs *both* binaries, so forgetting the flag clobbers stable — the scheme is only as safe as the flag discipline, where today's scheme is safe by default and requires an explicit act to touch `vc-x1`. If we taught `custom.md`'s validation line to always carry `--bin vc-x1-dev`, that edge is fenced but not removed.

My recommendation stays: constant manifest name, main-ness expressed at install time — with the two-`[[bin]]` variant as the honest middle path if the wrong-banner blemish bothers you enough to accept a flag-discipline risk. Either way it's a versioning.md template proposal for the iiac-perf discussion, and today's session is the evidence exhibit: a clobbered 0.79.0-0 install and a promoted binary bannering the wrong name.

The plain version: a commit can't know whether it's on main, because it's on a branch when written and on main after landing — same bytes. Forcing the name to differ by location means renaming twice per cycle, and worse, the routine pre-push validation would then overwrite everyone's stable binary with unpushed code. The safe versions of your idea all put the naming decision at install time — or, closest to your intent, define both binary names side by side in the manifest and pick by flag, accepting that a forgotten flag clobbers stable.

content.text:
Yes to the two-targets question — and it serves your goal better than the merge-edit, so let me do both halves.

**The merge-edit variant**: it genuinely fixes the boundary paradox *for merge-shaped landings* — a merge commit has its own tree, so it can carry the rename, and main's first-parent chain would consistently say `vc-x1`. But three costs follow. Every landing must then *be* a merge: 0.78.2 landed by fast-forward and 0.78.3 is about to, and `push` holds a stated invariant of never producing a merge (that's exactly why `trapezoid-push` is a separate command) — so plain landings would need empty merges just to host a rename. The pre-push validation clobber survives: the merge commit says `vc-x1`, and its mandatory `cargo install --path . --locked` runs before the push is approved, overwriting stable with unpublished code. And "working on main means name = `vc-x1`" makes it worse: every per-commit install during a directly-on-main cycle would overwrite the consumers' binary with rung-level code — the exact scenario that created the dev-name convention during 0.75.0.

**Two build targets: yes, and it's cleaner than I gave it credit for last message.** Cargo allows multiple `[[bin]]` sections pointing at the same `src/main.rs`:

```toml
[[bin]]
name = "vc-x1"
path = "src/main.rs"

[[bin]]
name = "vc-x1-dev"
path = "src/main.rs"
```

Both binaries build from identical source, the manifest is constant (no rename, ever, on any branch), and — the piece that fixes the banner blemish properly — the code's `BANNER` switches from `CARGO_PKG_NAME` to **`CARGO_BIN_NAME`**, which cargo sets per binary target at compile time. Then `vc-x1 -V` says `vc-x1 0.78.3` and `vc-x1-dev -V` says `vc-x1-dev 0.78.3`, from one tree, no clone trick.

The conventions that make it safe:

- **Per-commit flow installs `cargo install --path . --locked --bin vc-x1-dev`** — custom.md's validation line carries the flag. This is the scheme's one sharp edge: a bare `cargo install --path .` installs *both* binaries and clobbers stable. Cargo has no "default install target," so the flag is discipline, not enforcement; the flow's command string is the fence.
- **Promotion becomes one honest command**: at the landed main SHA, `cargo install --path . --locked --bin vc-x1`. Explicit act preserved, correct name, correct banner, no clone, no copy.
- **Your `devX` multiplicity stays install-time**: `[[bin]]` names are static manifest content, so per-branch `vc-x1-devX` entries would reintroduce the rename churn. When lines multiply, the differentiated copy (`vc-x1-dev-trapezoid`) remains the mechanism; `-V`'s version string is the identification either way.

Net: your invariant "installing gives you the proper name" holds — expressed as *which target you install*, which is a per-invocation fact, rather than *what the manifest says*, which is per-commit content that merges can't keep honest.

Process-wise this is a versioning.md "Dev artifact name" template proposal (pinned file, hard rule 12), with today as its evidence: the clobbered 0.79.0-0 install and the wrong-bannered promoted copy. The `[[bin]]` change itself plus the `CARGO_BIN_NAME` banner is a small vc-x1 cycle once the family agrees.

The plain version: editing the name at merge time only works if every landing is a merge, and it still lets routine validation overwrite the stable binary before anyone approved publishing. Declaring both binary names side by side in the manifest gets what you actually want — install produces the right name with the right self-report, from any commit — and the only cost is that install commands must always say which of the two they mean.

# Chores-16

Continuation of `chores-15.md` (closed after `0.78.0`, the jj-lib migration close-out). This
file covers `0.78.1` onward, back on `main` with the refactor program's long-lived bookmark
retired and the 20260803 baseline pin set in force. (`0.78.1` fell in the seam between the two
files and was originally recorded only in its TODO.md ladder rung and commit body; its section
below was added 2026-08-06, when the rung's narrative moved here.)

Reference numbering is file-local; see
[`agent-data/notes.md`](../../agent-data/notes.md#reference-numbering); chores-16 starts at
`[1]`.

## Table of Contents

- [docs: adopt the 20260803 baseline pin set](#docs-adopt-the-20260803-baseline-pin-set)
- [style: typeable punctuation + line-width source sweep](#style-typeable-punctuation--line-width-source-sweep)
- [refactor: drop sync state and remove revert](#refactor-drop-sync-state-and-remove-revert)

## docs: adopt the 20260803 baseline pin set

- [[2]] 0.78.1 docs: adopt the 20260803 baseline pin set

The instruction-set dedup, dogfooded ahead of iiac-perf's review of the 20260803 baseline; an
interlude between the refactor program's `0.78.0` and the `0.78.2` sweep. Its narrative
originally lived only in its TODO.md ladder rung, a seam decision this section reverses
(2026-08-06, at wink's ask): a ladder rung is an index entry, and when the index entry is the
only record, the narrative is invisible to anyone who looks where narratives live.

- the pin set: cycle-protocol.md + versioning.md pinned into `agent-data/` (moved from
  `notes/`, pinned-file headers added); jj-tips.md + draft-reviews.md deleted with their live
  content salvaged first (jj.md gains the Revsets primer and the long-lived-bookmark
  discipline, cycle-protocol.md the no-preflight-while-a-review-iterates rule); cycle.md
  renamed cycle-checklists.md (scope-collision fix at wink's review); every live link
  re-pointed
- README's "jj Tips for Git Users" became a signpost (jj.md quick reference, upstream
  tutorials, template-hosted jj-tips.md) instead of a drifting copy; it still said `obslog`,
  renamed `evolog` upstream, which is what a drifting copy does
- the dogfood log rehomed from custom.md to notes/dogfood.md: it is a record, and
  records-only placement puts it under `notes/`
- custom.md reset to the bare template skeleton in the same commit, no history lost (the log
  moved to notes/dogfood.md, the bookmark discipline pinned into jj.md, the rest was committed
  at `0.78.0`). The generic-custom.md test starts here: a project should not assume the
  template's location, name, or contents, so the project layer stays skeleton-identical and
  what breaks becomes dogfood findings in notes/dogfood.md

## style: typeable punctuation + line-width source sweep

- [[1]] 0.78.2 style: typeable punctuation + line-width source sweep

`src/` + `tests/` predate the typeable-punctuation rule and code.md's <=100-col comment wrap:
863 banned-character sites across 63 files and 60 overlong lines at pickup. A single-commit
cycle (wink's call at the opening review: the sweep is one homogeneous transformation, so a
ladder would checkpoint nothing a review gate and jj's op log don't already cover).

- the four named characters went to zero: `->` and `...` by mechanical replace, the 708 em
  dashes each given their structural decision (colon for term-elaboration, comma for
  continuation, parentheses for asides, sentence splits for contrasts), converted by four
  parallel lesser-model agents on disjoint file batches and audited after
- the sweep surfaced four *more* untypeable species the ban list does not name: `=>` was
  written `⇒` (13 sites), the config/show output drew rules with `─` (56), plus one `≥` and
  one U+2212 minus; all converted, output tests updated in the same pass (see the dogfood
  finding on the enumeration)
- the ellipsis in `truncate_chars` was load-bearing: appending one-char `…` kept truncated
  gists at cap+1, and the mechanical `...` conversion broke the length test; the function now
  reserves room for the suffix and stays within `max` (contract tightened, test to `<= CAP`)
- `config_cmd` section headers (`# ── x ──`) and `show`'s separator rule are user-visible
  output; they render as `-` runs now, and the README's config samples were regenerated from
  the installed binary so the docs match what the code emits
- line width: string literals split with backslash continuation (content byte-identical),
  comments re-wrapped, trailing `// OK:` comments moved above their statement where wrapping
  was awkward; exempt as literal rows: the JSONL fixture strings in the transcript /
  bot-session tests, and comment URLs

Riding in the same commit: the cycle records, the Done-retirement sweep of four
refactor-program entries into done.md, the `0.78.1` ladder-ref backfill, and the first
generic-custom.md-test findings logged in [notes/dogfood.md](../dogfood.md).

### Delegation notes

Four Sonnet agents converted the em-dash batches and a fifth did the line-width pass; two
incidents worth remembering when delegating sweeps:

- one batch agent "corrected" scope creep it thought it saw, reverting 29 already-converted
  arrows back to `→` because it compared against a pre-sweep baseline; caught by the
  post-batch character audit. A delegated sweep needs the invariant stated as "the end state
  is X", not "convert only Y": agents infer baselines
- the line-width agent first placed the continuation break-space after the backslash, which
  Rust strips with the leading whitespace, silently corrupting a fixture string; its own
  `cargo test` run caught it. String splits verify by test, not by eye

## refactor: drop sync state and remove revert

- [[N]] 0.78.3 refactor: drop sync state and remove revert

`sync-state.toml` was vc-x1's last cross-invocation state file, and this cycle removes the
species, not just the instance. The trigger was bugs.md #8 (2026-08-06): iiac-perf's `vc-x1`
0.71.0 push adopted a stale `push-state.toml`, skipped every stage but the last, and squashed a
new session into the previous cycle's published bot commit. Push's state machinery was already
deleted at 0.77.0-3; the same triage discussion concluded sync's snapshot file carries the same
disease and the backlog already knew it: the `## Todo` entry "Remove `revert`, and `.vc-x1/`
with it" had reached the identical verdict ("we are not in control enough to do this
reliably"). Decided by wink at the triage discussion, branched off `main` as a patch cycle
while `0.79.0` runs on its own bookmark.

- sync still snapshots each repo's pre-sync op id, in memory only: the snapshot exists to be
  printed by its own invocation's failure report, whose per-repo undo line is now the explicit
  `jj op restore <op> -R <repo>`
- `revert` is removed outright (first built as a disabled, explaining stub; wink asked for the
  keep-it argument at review and the argument lost: the teaching already lives at the only
  moment anyone reaches for revert, sync's failure report, and a CLI name is not a compat
  surface, so reintroduction is free if a safer design ever earns it)
- `init` stops writing `/.vc-x1` to new workspaces' `.gitignore` (both templates). Existing
  workspaces keep theirs: a report-not-rewrite check is deferred to the `## Todo` entry
  "Stale `/.vc-x1` gitignore line: report it, and a safer revert, if ever"
- the deleted `sync/state.rs` module comment was also the last place claiming push keeps a
  `push-state.toml`, a line bugs.md #8 had flagged as stale
- promoted to plain `vc-x1` at this cycle (wink, 2026-08-06), the first promotion since the
  dev-artifact-name convention: a copy of the `--locked`-installed dev binary, the explicit
  act versioning.md prescribes. The installed 0.71.0 was the actively dangerous default,
  carrying bugs #1, #4, and #8's stale-state machinery. Caveat: a copied binary still banners
  `vc-x1-dev` (name baked at compile time); the separate-clone path would banner `vc-x1`

### Why the file is unsound and the op log is not

The state file answers "where was the repo before the sync" and is blind to everything after
its write. `revert` ran `jj op restore` to it with no guard, so one commit after a failed
sync, "undo the sync" and "rewind to the snapshot" silently diverge and revert discards the
difference. No file-side fix closes that: presence-as-semaphore says nothing about intervening
operations.

jj's op log holds the same answer without the blindness: identify sync's operations, derive the
revert target as the parent of the most recent sync run's earliest op, and, decisively, detect
and refuse intervening non-sync operations. One honest prerequisite: only sync's fetch runs
through the in-process session today; its reposition and rebase steps still spawn the installed
jj (`jj new` / `jj rebase`, as do `op log` / `op restore` themselves), whose ops carry jj's
stock descriptions, so "identifiable sync operations" first means migrating those spawns, a
remainder 0.78.0's "ending jj and git subprocess spawning" claim reads as having finished but
did not (found 2026-08-06 at this cycle's review; tracked in the `## Todo` entry "Retire the
remaining jj spawns; make the build enforce it"). That derived-not-persisted design is the
bar any `revert` reintroduction must clear; until someone wants it, `jj op log` +
`jj op restore` is the documented recovery, shown by sync's failure report and README.

My sentence was badly compressed — let me untangle it, because the thing you want does work now.

**"Promotion" is not a feature and adds nothing to the banner.** It's just versioning.md's word for one specific act: installing the *stable* `vc-x1` binary. My sentence only meant "this time, stable `vc-x1` was installed using the new `--bin vc-x1` command." Nothing more. I'll rewrite that line in the description — if it confused you, it will confuse every later reader.

**You CAN have `vc-x1-dev-branch1` and `vc-x1-dev-branch2` side by side.** What's impossible is only the narrow thing: `cargo install` itself cannot *mint* those names, because bin names are fixed text in Cargo.toml. But a copy after install does it, and the banner change is exactly what makes the copies honest: the binary no longer bakes its name in at compile time — it reports whatever filename it was invoked as. The name on disk *is* the name in the banner. Per branch:

```
# while on branch1's working copy:
cargo install --path . --locked --bin vc-x1-dev
cp ~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1-dev ~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1-dev-branch1

# while on branch2's working copy:
cargo install --path . --locked --bin vc-x1-dev
cp ~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1-dev ~/.cargo/bin/vc-x1-dev-branch2
```

But could it be done using build.rs and have it get the current bookmark or maybe a name I provide on the cargo command line?

content.text:
The direct answer: cargo can't do it at build time — and the workaround you guessed at has a trap in this workflow specifically. But the no-manual-steps goal is reachable one level up. The pieces:

**Why build.rs can't**: target (and thus installed-file) names are static manifest text. A build script runs *before* compilation and can only emit compile inputs (env vars, cfgs, generated source); cargo has no post-build hook at all, so nothing in the build can see, move, or rename the finished binary. `cargo install` has no `--rename`. What build.rs *could* do is read the current bookmark (or an env var you pass like `VCX1_NAME=branch1 cargo install ...`) and bake it into the **banner** — but that changes what the binary *says*, not what the file is *called*, and the argv0 banner already solves the saying part more honestly.

**Why the local `bin.name` edit is a footgun here**: it works in an ordinary repo, but jj snapshots the working copy automatically — an uncommitted Cargo.toml rename rides straight into your next commit unless you remember to revert it first. In a workflow where `vc-x1 push` commits `@` as-is, a temporary manifest edit is exactly the kind of thing that publishes itself. I'd rule it out.

**The clean path: make vc-x1 its own installer.** A `vc-x1 install` subcommand is squarely in this tool's domain — it already knows the workspace and, in-process via jj-lib, the current bookmark:

```
vc-x1-dev install              # cargo install --bin vc-x1-dev, then places
                               #   vc-x1-dev-<current-bookmark> in ~/.cargo/bin
vc-x1-dev install --as branch1 # your chosen name instead
vc-x1-dev install --stable     # the promotion act, --bin vc-x1, main-SHA check built in
```

One command, no manual copy, name chosen or bookmark-derived, and it could *refuse* `--stable` off a landed main commit — turning the promotion convention into an enforced check instead of prose. Until it exists, the `cp` line (or a one-line shell alias/cargo alias wrapping it) is the interim.

This is a real subcommand, so it should not ride 0.78.3 — the cycle has absorbed two riders already. Recording it as a Todo:

content.text:
Thoughts only — and your instinct is pointing at something real: once `vc-x1 install` exists, the two `[[bin]]` targets stop earning their keep, and one of them is carrying a footgun.

**What the two names buy today**: promotion is a pure-cargo act — `cargo install --locked --bin vc-x1` — which means it's cargo-*tracked* (`cargo install --list` knows about stable, `--locked` provenance is native) and possible on a machine with no working vc-x1 at all. That's the whole benefit.

**What they cost**: the sharp edge we had to document in the manifest itself — a bare `cargo install --path .` installs *both* and clobbers stable. The safety of the whole scheme rests on never forgetting a flag. And once `install --stable` exists with its landed-main check, the cargo-native route becomes something worse than redundant: it's a *bypass* around the check — an unchecked way to mint stable that we'd keep alive purely for bookkeeping.

**The single-name world**: one `[[bin]] vc-x1-dev` (package stays `vc-x1`), argv0 banner unchanged. Then:

- Bare `cargo install --path . --locked` is **safe by default again** — it can only produce `vc-x1-dev`. No flag, no discipline, and the custom.md validation line goes back to its simple pre-0.78.3 form. The documented footgun disappears rather than being fenced.
- Stable `vc-x1` and every `-devX` become the same kind of thing: a *placement*, done by `vc-x1 install` (or the interim `cp`), with the argv0 banner making each placement self-truthful. One mechanism instead of two.
- Promotion gets exactly one road, and it's the checked one. The convention "only from a landed main SHA" stops having a side door.
- Bootstrap still works: fresh machine → `cargo install` gives `vc-x1-dev` → `vc-x1-dev install --stable` places `vc-x1`. No chicken-and-egg.

**What single-name gives up**: stable `vc-x1` becomes a file cargo doesn't track (no `cargo install --list` entry, no `cargo uninstall`), and pure-cargo promotion is gone — you need the tool or a copy. Both feel minor against removing the clobber hazard. One implementation detail: the CLI tests locate the binary via `CARGO_BIN_EXE_<package-name>`, which after the package rename resolves to the `vc-x1` target — single-name would point that at `vc-x1-dev` literally. Small, known, fixable.

**My take**: you're right — in the end state the two names are a bridge, and the bridge has a hole in it. The honest question is only *when*: simplify 0.78.3 now (drop the `vc-x1` target, keep the package rename and argv0 banner; today's promoted binary stays on disk untouched; interim promotion is the `cp`, which the banner keeps honest), or ship the two-target version and fold the target's removal into the `vc-x1 install` cycle. I lean **simplify now** — shipping a documented footgun that's already scheduled for demolition is the kind of thing we'd write a dogfood entry about later — but it's a genuine judgment call, and the two-target version does keep cargo-native promotion until #3 actually lands, which could be several cycles.

The plain version: the two names existed so cargo alone could produce both binaries safely-ish. Once your installer command is the blessed way to place *any* named binary, the second manifest name is just an unguarded spare key to stable. Keep one name in the manifest, let the installer hand out all the others — the open choice is whether to make that true in this commit or in the install cycle.

Say the word and I'll simplify in-cycle, or we push as-is.

content.text:
Your scheme holds together, and it's simpler than everything we've built this session. Here's what you're missing — one real hazard, two mechanical snags, and one refinement that makes your own idea cleaner:

**1. The failure you named is the mild one; the dangerous one is its mirror.** Forgetting the rename *at merge* leaves main with a dev name — cosmetic, as you say. But forgetting the rename *at cycle open* is the bad direction: you branch off main, the manifest still says `vc-x1`, and the per-commit validation's `cargo install` replaces your stable binary with rung-level dev code — the exact hazard the `-dev` suffix was invented for during 0.75.0. Same forgetfulness, asymmetric consequences. The mitigation is to make the rename a cycle-open records step, sitting right next to the version bump you already never skip (and a close-out step to rename back). Also note the close-out window: the pre-push validation install runs *as* `vc-x1` before the push is approved — if a push gets declined and amended, stable briefly holds an unpublished build. On a one-person machine that's recoverable-by-reinstall, but it's real.

**2. Refinement: rename the *package*, not a `[[bin]]` entry — then the `[[bin]]` stanzas disappear entirely.** With no explicit `[[bin]]`, cargo's default binary takes the package's name. And here's the part that makes this strictly better than a bin-name edit: the CLI tests locate the binary via `CARGO_BIN_EXE_<package-name>` — that macro *follows package renames automatically* (its own comment says "a Cargo.toml rename needs no edit here"), whereas a varying `[[bin]]` name would break it and force a runtime lookup helper. Costs of the package route: the name line in Cargo.lock churns per branch (a trivial conflict, same class as the version line), and `cargo update -p <name>` varies with the manifest — documented as "the name in Cargo.toml" rather than a literal.

**3. The family has to learn dynamic names.** custom.md's "invoke `vc-x1-dev`, never `vc-x1`" becomes "invoke the name in Cargo.toml" — the bot resolves it at acquaint (one manifest read). And a merge-forget isn't only your inconvenience: iiac-perf installing stable from main would get a dev-named binary and their instructions saying `vc-x1` would miss it. Mild, but tell them.

**4. Small print**: cargo's install bookkeeping keys on package name+source, so branch installs from the same checkout each get their own tracking entry under their own name — actually *cleaner* than today's same-package juggling. And the argv0 banner already in this diff stays useful unchanged: any name, manifest-born or copied, self-reports.

What you *gain* over everything previously discussed: no flag discipline, no copy step, no second target, no installer subcommand needed for the basic flow (Todo #3 shrinks to just the `--stable` landed-main *check*, if you ever want enforcement), promotion = `cargo install` from a main-positioned working copy, and per-branch coexistence is automatic because each branch's name is its own.

The plain version: one name, chosen in the manifest, works — provided the rename is a checklist step at cycle open (that's where forgetting hurts: it overwrites stable with dev code), and provided it's the *package* name you vary, because the test suite tracks that automatically while a bin-name edit would break it.

If you confirm, the 0.78.3 simplification is: delete both `[[bin]]` stanzas and the manifest comment (package `vc-x1`, default bin follows), keep the argv0 banner and all the wart fixes, revert the smoke-test anchor if desired (it's fine either way), update the records (chores rider rewritten to this final shape, the custom.md merge obligation simplified to `cargo update -p` and the rename-at-open/close checklist line, Todo #3 reduced to the `--stable` check idea), and re-run the gates. Say go and it's one pass.

Yes — as I proposed it, the guard is me (or you) following a checklist, and I should be honest about how much that's worth: your own records catalogue the failure rate of exactly that kind of guard. Three exhibits from this session alone: the version-first commit-body bullet was added to the protocol at 0.75.1 "because it was being missed" and slipped again at 0.78.2 (that's Todo #1); the program ladder's trunk-order invariant is "stated but nothing enforces it," which is how 0.78.2 went missing from it for three days; and the 0.78.0 "ending jj and git subprocess spawning" claim sailed through both of us reviewing it. I follow checklists well, and demonstrably not perfectly — and neither of us caught the misses until something else surfaced them. A safety property whose enforcement is "the bot remembers" is the pattern this project keeps writing dogfood entries about.

So if the single-name scheme goes in, the guard should be mechanical, and your workflow already has the place for it: **a name/branch coherence check that runs in the test gate, which precedes the install gate in both validation tiers**. Concretely: a small check (a `#[test]` gated on "this is the vc-x1 dev workspace", or a job for the committed cycle-check runner already in your Todo) that fails red when the manifest name and the line disagree, both directions:

- name is `vc-x1` but the working copy isn't sitting on main's tip → **fail before install ever runs**. This kills the dangerous case: forget the rename at cycle open, and the very first `cargo test` of the first rung goes red, instead of the install quietly replacing stable.
- name isn't `vc-x1` but the push target is main → caught at close-out validation, so the mild case (dev name landing on main) also stops being a memory game.

The residual that no repo check can cover: a bare `cargo install --path .` typed by hand outside the flow, on a wrongly-named tree. That's irreducible in your scheme — but it's also an explicit human act at that point, the same moral class as promotion itself, and the argv0 banner at least makes the resulting binary confess what it is.

The plain version: you asked the right question — "the bot follows AGENTS.md" is a guard made of good intentions, and this repo's own history shows those leak about once a week. The fix isn't a better checklist, it's putting the check where the machinery already runs: the name-vs-branch test that fails validation before the install step can do damage. With that, your single-name scheme keeps its simplicity and gets a real guard.

Practically: the check is small and belongs with the scheme, so I'd fold both into the 0.78.3 simplification — single name, argv0 banner kept, coherence check in the test gate — or, if you'd rather keep this cycle as-is, queue the whole single-name move as its own entry. Your call.

- promoted to plain `vc-x1` at this cycle (wink, 2026-08-06), the first promotion since the
  dev-artifact-name convention: first as a binary copy, then through an interim dual-`[[bin]]`
  target, finally as the single-name scheme's ordinary `cargo install --path . --locked` from
  this close-out tree. The `--force` along the way transferred cargo's install-ownership
  record from the old stable, `vc-x1 v0.71.0` built from a separate plain-named checkout
  (`../vc-x1-main`), which is how promotion worked before this cycle. The installed 0.71.0
  was the actively dangerous default, carrying bugs #1, #4, and #8's stale-state machinery

### The single-name convention

Settled across one review conversation (wink, 2026-08-06), through three designs, each
killed by its own sharp edge:

- **manifest-name-per-branch-location** ("on main say vc-x1, on a branch say dev") fails
  structurally: a commit is on a branch when authored and on main after landing,
  byte-identical, so no committed name can track location, and the rename-at-merge variant
  forces every landing to be a merge while still letting pre-push validation clobber stable
- **dual `[[bin]]` targets** (`vc-x1` + `vc-x1-dev` over one `src/main.rs`, install by
  `--bin`) shipped briefly inside this cycle and was discarded at review: the second name is
  an unguarded spare key to stable, since a bare `cargo install --path .` installs both, and
  the whole scheme rests on never forgetting a flag
- **single name** (adopted): the package name IS the installed binary's name. `vc-x1` on
  main; a per-line dev name on a branch, renamed at cycle open and back at close-out, next to
  the version bump those steps already make. No `[[bin]]` stanzas at all; the CLI tests'
  `CARGO_BIN_EXE_<package-name>` lookup tracks renames automatically; promotion is an
  ordinary install from a main-positioned tree; concurrent dev lines coexist because each
  line's manifest names its own binary

The guard is mechanical because the procedural record is bad: the version-first commit
bullet slipped twice past the checklist, the ladder's trunk-order invariant is "stated but
nothing enforces it", and 0.78.0's over-claim survived two reviewers.
`dev_rung_never_wears_the_stable_name` (src/version.rs) asserts from compile-time facts that
a suffixed version, which marks a dev rung, never carries the stable package name; it sits
in the test gate, which precedes the install gate in both validation tiers, so a forgotten
open-rename goes red before an install can replace stable with unpushed code. The mild
direction (a dev name reaching main under a bare version) stays procedural on purpose:
enforcing it would fail branch close-outs that rename at their merge commit. The residual
nobody can catch: a hand-typed install from a wrongly-named tree, which is an explicit act,
the same moral class as promotion.

**The banner is the invoked name, at runtime**: `argv[0]`'s basename + version, replacing the
compile-time `CARGO_PKG_NAME` constant (with `CARGO_BIN_NAME` as the empty-argv fallback), so
renames and copies self-report whatever they run as, verified with `vc-x1-dev-dropsync
0.78.3`. The smoke test's banner-leak assertions anchor on the version string, the banner's
one invocation-independent marker. Two warts surfaced dogfooding it, both fixed: the bare
invocation stacked the ambient banner over help's about line (ambient now skips when no
subcommand was given), and the manual `print_help` path fell back to the package name in its
usage line (`bin_name` now set from the invoked name).

This overrides versioning.md "Dev artifact name" in mechanism, not intent; dogfooded here
first, the template proposal follows.

The final state of the naming saga is in: no `[[bin]]` stanzas at all, the package name is the binary name, the coherence test guards the dangerous direction, and the chores design subsection now tells the three-design evolution honestly (including that the dual-`[[bin]]` scheme shipped briefly inside this cycle and why it died). One operational note for you: **`vc-x1-dev` is gone from your PATH** — cargo pruned it when the single-name reinstall redefined the package's binary set. The full, final description:

---

**Title**: `refactor: drop sync state and remove revert`

**Body**:

```
Sync keeps no state across invocations and revert is gone. The
trigger is bugs.md #8: a stale state file adopted by a later
invocation is how push corrupted published history at 0.71.0, and
sync-state.toml was the last file of that species. Riding along,
the single-name convention: the package name is the installed
binary's name (vc-x1 on main, per-line dev names on branches),
guarded by a compile-time coherence test; the banner reports the
invoked name at runtime; and stable vc-x1 was promoted from this
tree. Narrative, the safer-revert bar, and the naming design's
evolution in chores-16 "refactor: drop sync state and remove
revert".

- Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock: v0.78.3
  - package renamed vc-x1-dev -> vc-x1: the manifest name IS the
    binary's name, renamed to a per-line dev name at cycle open
    and back at close-out, beside the version bump; no [[bin]]
    stanzas; plain `cargo install --path . --locked` installs
    exactly one, correctly named binary
- src/version.rs: dev_rung_never_wears_the_stable_name, the
  convention's mechanical guard: a suffixed version (a dev rung)
  must not carry the stable package name; compile-time facts
  only, sitting in the test gate, which precedes the install
  gate in both validation tiers
- src/sync/state.rs: deleted; the persisted pre-sync snapshot
  module and its tests
- src/sync.rs
  - op-id snapshots in memory only, living for this invocation's
    failure report; the save/clear calls gone with the module
  - failure report's undo line is the explicit
    `jj op restore <op> -R <repo>`
  - module and orchestrator docs: nothing persists across
    invocations
- src/revert.rs: deleted; removed rather than stubbed (sync's
  failure report carries the recovery at the moment of need;
  reintroduction is free if an op-log-derived design earns it)
- src/main.rs
  - Revert variant, dispatch arm, and module gone; sync
    long_about points at the manual op restore
  - BANNER / TOP_ABOUT constants become banner() / top_about():
    argv[0]'s basename + version at runtime (CARGO_BIN_NAME as
    empty-argv fallback), so renamed manifests and copied
    binaries alike self-report the name they run as
  - ambient banner skipped when no subcommand was given (help's
    about line already opens with the same text); bin_name set
    from the invoked name, so the no-subcommand usage line says
    the name you ran, not the package name

- src/init/tests.rs: templates asserted to not contain `/.vc-x1`

- [License](#license)

This is experiment 1 to explore creating a Vibe Coding (vc) environment. We will investigate ways of
using the dual jj-git repo concept, explored in
===
## Terminology

A vc-x1 workspace pairs two jj-git repos, and this README names their two sides **work** and
**bot**:

- **work repo**: the repo at the project root, holding the work product itself (source code, docs,
  the repo you would have anyway).
- **bot repo**: the `.claude` repo nested inside it, holding the bot's session data (the
  conversation that produced the work).
- **work** / **bot**: the two sides as roles, used wherever a command or doc needs to say which repo
  it means (e.g. push's `commit-work` / `commit-bot` stages).

A few naming conventions this project keeps, to avoid ambiguous jargon:

- **path** is reserved for a filesystem location, qualified as **relative** or **absolute** when it
  matters (e.g. `../other`, `/home/you/repo`).
- a configuration setting is a **config key**, e.g. `bot-session.col-width` (its TOML table and key
  joined by `.`); not a "path".
- a datum in a transcript's `--fields` inventory is a **field**, e.g. `message.content[].type`, its
  levels joined by `.`, with `[]` marking array elements.

## Usage

```
vc-x1 list [-r REVISION] [-n COMMITS]  # List commits in a jj repo
vc-x1 desc [-r REVISION] [-n COMMITS]  # Show full description of a commit
vc-x1 chid [-r REVISION] [-n COMMITS]  # Print changeID(s) for a revision

This is experiment 1 to explore creating a Vibe Coding (vc) environment. We will investigate ways of
using the dual jj-git repo concept, explored in
===
## Terminology

A vc-x1 workspace pairs two jj-git repos, and this README names their two sides **work** and
**bot**:

- **work repo**: the repo at the project root, holding the work product itself (source code, docs,
  the repo you would have anyway).
- **bot repo**: the `.claude` repo nested inside it, holding the bot's session data (the
  conversation that produced the work).
- **work** / **bot**: the two sides as roles, used wherever a command or doc needs to say which repo
  it means (e.g. push's `commit-work` / `commit-bot` stages).

A few naming conventions this project keeps, to avoid ambiguous jargon:

- **path** is reserved for a filesystem location, qualified as **relative** or **absolute** when it
  matters (e.g. `../other`, `/home/you/repo`).
- a configuration setting is a **config key**, e.g. `bot-session.col-width` (its TOML table and key
  joined by `.`); not a "path".
- a datum in a transcript's `--fields` inventory is a **field**, e.g. `message.content[].type`, its
  levels joined by `.`, with `[]` marking array elements.

## Usage

```
vc-x1 list [-r REVISION] [-n COMMITS]  # List commits in a jj repo
vc-x1 desc [-r REVISION] [-n COMMITS]  # Show full description of a commit
vc-x1 chid [-r REVISION] [-n COMMITS]  # Print changeID(s) for a revision

## Build and install

A plain Rust crate: `cargo build`, `cargo test`, and

```
cargo install --path . --locked
```

installs one binary named by the manifest's `[package].name`. That name is deliberate, the
**single-name convention** (adopted 0.78.3; design record in
`notes/chores/chores-16.md`):

- On `main` the name is `vc-x1`: installing from a main-positioned tree gives you the stable
  binary, and that is the whole promotion ceremony.
- A development line renames `[package].name` to its own name (e.g. `vc-x1-dev`,
  `vc-x1-<topic>`) at cycle open and back to `vc-x1` at close-out, next to the version bump
  those steps already make. Each line's install then produces its own binary, and concurrent
  lines coexist on `PATH` under their own names.
- The guard is mechanical, not memory: the `dev_rung_never_wears_the_stable_name` test fails
  any tree whose version carries a dev suffix (`0.79.1-2`) while the manifest still says
  `vc-x1`, and the test gate runs before the install gate in the validation flow, so a
  forgotten rename goes red before an install can replace your stable binary.
- The binary banners the name it was invoked as (`argv[0]`), so a renamed manifest, a copy,
  or a symlink all self-report truthfully; the version in the banner identifies the exact
  commit either way.

vc-x1 links jj-lib and refuses to run when the installed `jj`'s version disagrees with it
(override per invocation with `--allow-jj-mismatch`; see `vc-x1 version`).

content.text:
Your matrix matches the design intent exactly, and the fourth quadrant is the interesting one. My thoughts, then I'll fold your experiment into the README as the worked example.

**Quadrant 3 (`vc-x1-exper1` + bare `0.78.3`) should pass, and your reason is the right one** — the stable binary is not at risk; installing from that tree produces `vc-x1-exper1`, which clobbers nothing and confesses its name in the banner. But there's a second, structural reason it *must* pass: the trapezoid flow. A branch that lands by merge does its rename *in the merge commit*, which means the branch's own close-out commit is legitimately bare-versioned under a dev name — and close-out is exactly where full validation is mandatory. Hard-failing quadrant 3 would red every trapezoid close-out's gate, including 0.79.0's a few cycles from now.

**"But it could?" — yes, and the harm it guards would be different in kind.** Quadrant 1's harm is *install-time*: dev code replaces your stable binary the moment validation runs. Quadrant 3's harm is *landing-time*: if that commit reaches main as-is, main's manifest names the wrong binary and someone installing stable gets `vc-x1-exper1`. Confusing, self-announcing, recoverable — and crucially, the harm happens at a different site. Which suggests the principled answer: each direction gets guarded where its harm occurs. Install-time harm → test gate, before install (built). Landing-time harm → *push*, which unlike any test knows the target bookmark: `vc-x1 push main` with a manifest name other than `vc-x1` could refuse or ask. A test can never know where a commit is headed; push always does. That's the mechanical home for quadrant 3 if it ever wants one — cheap to add whenever push grows its next validation. Recording that thought in the chores subsection, and your matrix in the README:

The plain version of my answer to your question: you're right, and for two reasons — that tree endangers no installed binary, and the trapezoid flow *requires* dev-name-plus-bare-version to be legal, because merge-landing branches rename in the merge commit itself. content.text: Right — and that's a hole, not a footnote: `cargo install` never runs tests, so a hand-typed install skips the guard entirely, and my "the test gate precedes the install gate" only holds if you follow the flow. The proper fix closes it completely: move the check into **`build.rs`**, which runs on *every* cargo verb — build, clippy, test, and crucially `cargo install` itself. Then the forbidden quadrant can't even compile, and the guard stops depending on anyone's discipline. Implementing:

lines: -//! Export the resolved `jj-lib` version as `JJ_LIB_VERSION`.
-//! jj-lib exports no version constant of its own, so the only
-//! statement of what this binary links against is the resolved
-//! version in `Cargo.lock`:
-//! - the lock is read from `$CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR` directly, not by
-//!   walking ancestors: we are not a workspace, and a walk can
-//!   bind a sibling project's lock, which is worse than failing.
-//! - a missing or jj-lib-less lock fails the build rather than
-//!   emitting an "unknown" that would later be reported as fact.
+//! The single-name convention's guard (chores-16, 0.78.3): a
+//! suffixed version marks a dev rung, and a dev rung must never
+//! carry the stable package name, or installing it replaces the
+//! stable `vc-x1` binary with unpushed code. Living here rather
+//! than in a `#[test]` because `cargo install` never runs tests:
+//! a build script runs on every cargo verb, so the forbidden
+//! combination fails to compile at all, install included.
-use std::path::Path;
-/// Extract `jj-lib`'s resolved version from `Cargo.lock` text.
-/// Scans for the `[[package]]` block whose `name` is `jj-lib` and
-/// returns that block's `version`. Line-based rather than a TOML

It's good — terse, causal, and letting cargo's prefix carry the version was the right call. Two thoughts, one substantive:

**"refusing to install" is verb-inaccurate for most of the ways this fires.** The guard runs on *every* cargo verb — someone in the forbidden quadrant sees this message from `cargo build`, `cargo test`, or clippy, where "refusing to install" reads confusingly, since they weren't installing anything. The fix is one word: "so refusing to **build** `vc-x1` as it is the stable binary name." Install stays covered (an install *is* a build), and the message is true in every context that shows it.

**Minor, take or leave**: line 2's reason is slightly circular — it re-states the naming fact ("as it is the stable binary name") rather than the harm (dev code overwriting your stable binary). Your earlier instinct to cut the "clobber" verbiage was right for terseness, and the README carries the full story, so I'd leave this alone unless "as installing it would replace the stable binary" reads better to you.

So my proposal is your text with the single word swapped:

error: vc-x1@0.78.3-x: A suffixed version is used with the stable package name, `vc-x1`
error: vc-x1@0.78.3-x: so refusing to build `vc-x1` as it is the stable binary name.
```

Whichever you pick, the README's example block needs syncing to the final text (it still shows the previous wording) — say the word ("mine as-is" or "with build") and I'll sync it, re-run the gates, and we're back at the description-then-push gates.

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
[Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit.
4. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
5. Say "ready to commit" and stop. The user reviews the working-copy diff; iterate until
   complete.
6. Write the description: a <=50-col conventional title, then a problem statement and a solution
   statement, both broad, wrapped at <=72. No version in either, no file list (the diff is the
   mechanical record), and no deliberation (chores, todo, and the session hold that). See
   [Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
7. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
8. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

content.content:
## Commit description

[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):

```
<type>: <short description>
```

**A commit names no version**, in its title or its body. The version-of-record (where it lives
and its bump cadence, see [versioning.md](versioning.md)) is useful for confirming you are
running the version you are testing; it is not an identifier, and a commit already records it in
the manifest. Writing it into the description copies it into text that cannot be edited: a
version is only stable once it lands on the permanent branch, and even then a history rewrite may
renumber it, at which point every description naming it is wrong forever. See
[Versions live in the version-of-record only](../agent-data/prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).

### Title

- <=50 chars total.
- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`.
- Favor terse phrasings.
- **Distinct per step**: each of a cycle's commits gets its own descriptive title (no shared
  cycle title with a step marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles (e.g.
  `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them; the chores section header matches the
  close-out title.
- **Unambiguous where it is resolved**: the title is the only identifier a record has, so it must
  be distinct within its cycle and within its chores file (a `##` header is also an anchor). It
  may repeat across the repo's history. See
  [Steps are named, not numbered](../agent-data/prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).

### Body

A **problem statement** then a **solution statement**, in
[Prose form](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets), wrapped <=72. The problem
statement says what was wrong and defines any word the title assumes; the solution statement says
what was done about it. Content rules, including why the body carries no file list, are in
[agent-data/prose.md](../agent-data/prose.md#prose-form) and are not repeated here.

Two repo-specific points:

- **Work-repo body**: the problem is the artifact's or the records' problem.
- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: the statements describe in-session activity rather than
  work-repo changes.

### Trailer

`ochid:` as the last line of the body; see
[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](../AGENTS.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
in AGENTS.md for the convention.

For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows; the
hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.

## Reviewing changes

content.text:
Read in full — their checklist item, the protocol section, and the prose.md rationale behind it. My thoughts: **adopt it**, and this session is close to a controlled experiment proving why.

**The case for, with our own evidence attached:**

1. **This cycle is the exhibit.** The 0.78.3 body went through five redrafts tonight, one per rider, ~90 lines of me hand-summarizing a diff you had *already reviewed* at the ready-to-commit gate. Under problem/solution, the body would have survived nearly every rider untouched — the problem never changed, and the solution statement would have absorbed each rider in a clause.

2. **Their drift argument has our fingerprints on it.** "A second copy that can drift from the first" is exactly how the 0.78.0 over-claim happened: "ending jj and git subprocess spawning" was body prose asserting more than the diff did, and it survived review *because the prose is what got read*. The diff cannot over-claim; a hand-written file list can, and mine tonight surely contains small paraphrase inaccuracies nobody will ever audit.

3. **Their version argument has our exhibit too.** "A history rewrite may renumber it, at which point every description naming it is wrong forever" — that's the 0.72.0 gap's logic: you accepted a hole in the version sequence precisely because renumbering would have rewritten cross-linked history. And the version-first bullet is the single most-slipped rule in your records: Todo #1 exists *because* it was missed at 0.75.1's adoption and again at 0.78.2. Adopting this dissolves that half of Todo #1 the honest way — not a sharper guardrail, no bullet to forget.

4. **One home per text, completed.** Mechanics in the diff (immutable, exact), narrative in chores, state in TODO, deliberation in the session the ochid names. Our current shape keeps mechanics in two places; theirs finishes the principle your notes conventions already preach.

**The costs, honestly:** the at-a-glance version in log viewers goes away (mitigated by the manifest diff each commit carries, and `git log -S'version = "..."'`; their renumbering argument cuts deeper the other way). File-name grep in `git log --grep` goes away (but `jj log <path>` does that natively and better). And it cascades through pinned files — cycle-checklists step 7, cycle-protocol's Commit description, prose.md, and notes.md's "the commit body is the mechanical record" doctrine — so the adoption path is the now-standard dance: custom.md override naming the superseded sections, dogfood here, template proposal folded into the 20260803 baseline review, where this also corrects the 08-05 message's claim that the repos contradict on no rule — they contradict on exactly this one.

**For this commit specifically**: applied now, the body collapses to a problem statement (cross-invocation state proved poisonous at 0.71.0, sync-state.toml was the last of the species, and the naming/promotion conventions had no governance), a solution statement (in-memory snapshots, revert removed, the single-name convention with its build.rs guard, the argv0 banner, the records), and the `BREAKING-CHANGE:` trailer — roughly fifteen lines, written once, stable against everything tonight threw at it.

The plain version: their rule says the diff already is the perfect file list and the manifest already is the version, so the commit message should carry the one thing neither can — why. Tonight's five redrafts of a ninety-line body are the strongest argument I can offer; I'd adopt, starting with this very commit.

On your word: I'll add the custom.md override, redraft the description in the new shape, finish the interrupted test-gate check (fmt and clippy are already green after restoring your experiment's leftover `0.78.3-x` — which, note, the new guard caught all by itself), and we're back at the two gates.

All records validate. Here is the description redrafted under the newly adopted convention — its first dogfood:

---

**Title** (43 cols): `refactor: drop sync state and remove revert`

**Body**:

```
Cross-invocation state files describe a world that may have
changed for reasons the tool cannot know. Push's copy of the
disease published a session under the wrong commit (bugs.md #8);
sync's copy, sync-state.toml, was the last one: a pre-sync
snapshot that revert would blindly restore, discarding any work
recorded after the failed sync it meant to undo. Nearby, nothing
governed the installed binary's name: promotion to a stable vc-x1
was a hand copy, and an ordinary dev install could silently
replace the stable binary.

Sync now snapshots pre-sync op ids in memory only and prints them
in its failure report with the explicit per-repo `jj op restore`
recovery; revert is removed, reintroducible only behind an
op-log-derived design that can refuse intervening work. The
manifest's package name is now the binary's name, vc-x1 on main
and a per-line dev name on branches, enforced by the build
script, which refuses a suffixed version under the stable name on
every cargo verb; the banner reports the invoked name at runtime.
The gitignore templates stop writing the now-empty state
directory, and the README gains the build, install, and naming
instructions.

BREAKING-CHANGE: the revert subcommand is removed; after a failed
sync, recover per repo with `jj op log` then
`jj op restore <op> -R <repo>`
```

**Body**:

```
`.vc-x1/sync-state.toml` recorded a pre-sync snapshot for
`vc-x1 revert` to restore, but nothing guaranteed that record was
still valid for the repo's current state, so a revert could
silently discard later work. It was the last cross-invocation
state file, and the same disease in push had already published a
session under the wrong commit (bugs.md #8).

- Sync wrote the snapshot before acting and cleared it only on
  full success, so a failed sync left it behind indefinitely.
- Revert restored it blindly: one commit after the failed sync,
  "undo the sync" and "rewind to the snapshot" are different
  things, and revert discarded the difference.
- Nearby, nothing governed the installed binary's name: promotion
  to a stable vc-x1 was a hand copy, and an ordinary dev install
  could silently replace the stable binary.

Nothing is trusted across invocations now, in state or in name.

  in the failure report with the explicit per-repo
  `jj op restore` recovery.
- Revert is removed; any reintroduction must derive its target
  from the op log and refuse when unrelated operations sit in
  between.
- The manifest's package name is now the binary's name: vc-x1 on
  main, a per-line dev name on branches. build.rs refuses a
  suffixed version under the stable name on every cargo verb, and
  the banner reports the invoked name at runtime.
- The gitignore templates stop writing the now-empty state
  directory, and the README gains build, install, and naming
  instructions.

BREAKING-CHANGE: the revert subcommand is removed; after a failed
sync, recover per repo with `jj op log` then
`jj op restore <op> -R <repo>`
```

content.text:
Sound plan, and the `/exit`-first variant is the better one. The pieces check out:

**`vc-x1 squash-push` from inside `.claude` is the documented tool for exactly this state** — it's what `validate-bot` prescribes for "main moved but unpublished," and it does precisely what the failed `squash-push-bot` stage would have: fold `@`'s accumulated session tail into the bot commit (`@-`), advance `main`, push. The squash rewrites the commit id but not the change id, and the work commit's `ochid:` names the change id, so the pairing survives untouched. The remote never saw the unpushed commit, so the push is a plain fast-forward of the full stream — same size, but from the shell that succeeds.

**`/exit` first is worth it here**: it closes the transcript, so the 0.78.3 bot commit carries this session *complete* — the bug report, the whole naming saga, and its own ending — instead of the tail riding into the next cycle's bot commit. Without `/exit` it still works (a spanning tail is the normal steady state), but this session is a good one to keep whole, and the cycle owes nothing more in-session: the follow-ups (backfill 0.78.3's refs at the next push, delete `drop-sync-state-vc-x1`, the iiac-perf mailbox update about stable 0.78.3 and the description convention, the uncommitted `../vc-x1-template` mailbox files) are all natural acquaint work for the next session.

One nit for the record you won't need: no `--force`-anything is required — and notably, nothing about this recovery involves clearing state or `--restart`, because there is no state. The failure you're recovering from is the last one of its kind that can leave anything behind.

So: `/exit`, then from `.claude`: `vc-x1 squash-push`. See you next session.
